events.text: A hard frost, and the river freezes clear as a window. You look down through it at the water and see yourself from above for the first time in a century: the shell has gone black. Not brown, not dark green, black, with a dull shine to it like an inkstone that has just been wiped. When the snake drags its chin across one plate it leaves a grey line, the way a stick of ink does on wet stone. The snake is delighted. "We could write on anything now," it says. The tortoise is not delighted. Things written on stone stay written.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie still on the ice all winter and let the black set slowly, all the way through

effects.log: You lie on the ice until the snow covers you and the river people take you for a black rock. By spring the black has gone right through, plate by plate. The snake spent the winter drawing on the snow with its tail, and says the snow does not count.

choices.text: The snake: write a character it learned long ago on a flat river stone, just to see

effects.log: Water, the character, three strokes and a hook. It sits on the stone in grey for a month and the fishermen walk round it. The tortoise says nothing about it all winter, which from the tortoise is a long speech.

choices.text: Both heads: write one character together, the snake's stroke and the tortoise's weight

effects.log: The snake draws, the tortoise presses. The character is Long, as in a long life, and it is the first thing either of you has ever made that the other could not have made alone. It is still on that stone. It will be for a while.

events.text: Every spring you shed a few old scutes, thin black plates of horn, and the river takes them. This year one of them washes up at the door of {npc}, a scholar who failed the capital examination three times and came to live in a reed hut by the ford to copy books for the villages. {He} grinds your scute on an inkstone out of curiosity. The ink is blacker than any pine-soot stick in the county and smells, faintly, of river ice. {npc} wades along the bank all week, turning over stones, looking for more.

choices.text: Leave your shed scutes on the hut's doorstep every spring

mem.note: left me ink on my step every spring

effects.log: Every spring {npc} opens the door and finds three or four black scutes on the step, still wet. {He} never asks who leaves them. {He} starts leaving a rice ball on the step in the autumn. The snake eats it.

choices.text: The snake: show itself in the shallows and ask {him} what {he} means to write with it

effects.log: "Genealogies," {npc} says, once {he} can speak again. "For families whose houses burned. They come to me and tell me who their grandfathers were, and I write it down." The snake considers this a fair use. The tortoise considers it the only use.

choices.text: The tortoise: draw in and let the river keep its own scutes

effects.log: You lie shut under the ford while {npc} searches. {He} finds one more scute, by luck, and makes it last three years. The snake says, from inside the shell, that this is a waste of a good customer.

events.text: {npc}'s ink has become a small legend in three counties: genealogies written in it do not fade, do not run in a flood, and the paper goes brittle before the characters do. Now a well-dressed visitor has come to the reed hut with an offer of a tiled house for the rest of the ink. {npc} comes down to the water at dusk, troubled. "The visitor wants it for seals," {npc} says. "Land deeds. Ink that never fades makes a very good forgery."

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "Ink from my back writes only what is true. Say so, and let the forger try"

effects.log: The visitor buys two scutes anyway and forges eleven deeds. Within a year every forged seal has cracked across, clean through the paper, like a plate in the frost. The magistrate is very interested in the cracks. The snake is very pleased with the tortoise, and says so, which is rarer than the cracks.

choices.text: The snake: "Sell the forger the old scutes. Keep the new ones for the genealogies"

effects.log: {npc} gets a tiled roof and the visitor gets brittle old scutes that grind to grey. Everyone is a little cheated and nobody is ruined. The tortoise says nothing for a season. It is the loudest nothing you have heard in a century.

choices.text: Both heads: tell {npc} to refuse, and to write the forger's own genealogy, truthfully, for free

effects.log: The forger reads the forger's own grandfather's name in ink that will not fade, and the grandfather's debts, and the grandfather's gaol term, all true. The forger leaves the county. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down in the reeds.

events.text: {npc} is dying in the reed hut, old and very thin, with forty years of genealogies stacked to the rafters. A grandchild comes down to the ford with the inkstone wrapped in hemp: worn into a deep black bowl by your scutes. "Grandfather said to give it back to the river," the child says. "Grandfather said the river would know what that means."

choices.text: Take the inkstone down to the riverbed and keep it under you

effects.log: It lies under your plastron for ages and never goes dry. Sometimes, in the long winters, you dream in characters.

choices.text: The snake: tell the child to keep it, and to come back when the ink runs out

effects.log: The child keeps it, and grows up to copy genealogies in the reed hut, and comes back to the ford every spring for scutes. The family never runs out of ink, or of customers.

events.text: The snake asks, one night under the ice, where the river comes from. Not this stretch: the river. All rivers. The tortoise has lived on water for three hundred years and has never once wondered. Now it cannot stop. For the first time in your life, both heads want the same thing at the same moment, and it frightens you both a little: to go north, to where the water starts.

choices.text: Both heads: go now, before either of you can change its mind

effects.log: You leave the ford at the thaw. The ferry people put out a bowl of millet for a month, in case. The snake says they will be glad of the rest.

choices.text: The tortoise: go, but properly, one river at a time, however many years it takes

effects.log: You go up the river the way a tortoise goes anywhere, at the speed of moss. The snake complains every li, and counts every li, and you both notice that it has not once asked to turn back.

choices.text: The snake: send the snow geese to ask first, and go when they answer

effects.log: The geese go north and do not come back, which the snake takes for an answer. You set off the following spring. The tortoise points out that it would have set off anyway.

events.text: Upriver for years: past the last rice paddies, past the last millet, to villages where people salt fish in barrels and wear dog-skin hats and the women chop holes in the ice to draw water. Then a gorge, and in the gorge a waterfall frozen solid from top to bottom, a pillar of white as tall as a pagoda. The snake has gone stiff and slow in the cold. It is a snake, after all. It cannot go into the shell the way you can.

choices.text: The tortoise: draw the snake in close under the rim of the shell and go on very slowly

effects.log: You go up beside the frozen fall a hand's width at a time, with the snake pressed flat against your neck. It does not say thank you. It does not have to. (-5 health)

choices.text: The snake: go on outside, stiff or not; it wants to see

effects.log: The snake sees the frozen fall with fish caught inside the ice like flies in amber, and the stars over the gorge. It also nearly dies. It says, once it can speak, that it would do it again. (-10 health)

choices.text: Shelter a decade in a hot spring the hunters use, and let the snake thaw

effects.log: A steaming pool among rocks, monkeys on the far side, a hunter who comes to bathe every autumn and thinks you are a very lucky stone. The snake would stay for ever. You leave after ten years, warm all through.

events.text: The river gives out, and beyond it lies a sea, and the sea is white. Ice to the edge of the sky, ridged and blue in the cracks, and on it the snow geese gathering in their thousands before they go south, so loud the ice hums. One old goose, grey at the beak, walks over to you on the ice and looks at both your heads in turn. "Two," it says. "I have seen everything that comes north, and I have never seen two."

choices.text: Ask the old goose to carry words south for you, now and then

effects.log: The goose considers it a reasonable request from a creature with two heads. "Every autumn," it says. "Short words. Geese do not do long ones." From then on the snow geese of that flock will carry for you, and so will their grandchildren.

choices.text: The tortoise: go down under the sea ice and sleep one whole northern winter

effects.log: Black water under white ice, so cold that time goes thick. You sleep, and the winter that comes out of the north sea goes over you and into you, and when you wake it has a little of your shape.

choices.text: The snake: eat the goose. It is a long way home

effects.log: The snake is quick and the goose is old. The flock lifts off the ice all at once with a noise like the sea breaking, and never comes within a li of you again. The tortoise says nothing. The snake says that the tortoise was hungry too, which is true, and does not help.

events.text: On the longest night the sky over the white sea begins to move: green curtains, then red at the hem, shaking out over the pole. And behind them, very clear, seven dark stars in a line, as straight as a bench, with a space in the middle where something should be sitting and is not. You know what it is without being told. The Northern Palace of heaven, the seven mansions of the north, and its seat. Empty. "Who sat there last?" the snake asks. The tortoise does not know.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie on the ice and look at it all night without blinking

effects.log: You look until the aurora fades and the seven stars go back to being only stars. The tortoise has not blinked once. In the morning it says: "Nobody, for a long time." It is not sure how it knows.

choices.text: The snake: count the stars aloud, every one, the dark ones too

effects.log: Dipper, Ox, Girl, Emptiness, Rooftop, Encampment, Wall. The snake counts them all night, over and over, in case one of them changes. None does. It is very satisfying and very sad.

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise looks and the snake counts, all night, together

effects.log: The tortoise looks up at the northern sky without blinking and the snake counts aloud, and somewhere in the night you realise you are doing something that will be done again, a great many times, by you. You do not know yet what it is for.

events.text: A fire on the ice. A very old person sits beside it on a sledge-frame, wrapped in deer hide, with a drum on {his} knees and a face like a walnut: {npc}, a shaman of the people who herd deer at the edge of the white sea. {He} is not surprised to see you. "So," {npc} says. "The north has sent its tortoise at last. My grandmother's grandmother said the winters went wrong because nobody kept them. Are you going to keep them?"

choices.text: The snake: "Who kept them before?"

effects.log: "A black thing with two minds," {npc} says, "like you. It quarrelled with itself and went to pieces, and the pieces became the hills to the east." {He} drums once. "That is a story. I do not know if it is true. You will find out."

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "I do not know yet. I am slow"

mem.note: said you did not know yet

effects.log: {npc} laughs, a dry crack like ice. "Good," {he} says. "The fast ones never last up here." {He} gives you a strip of dried fish, which the snake takes, and the blessing of the north, which the tortoise does.

choices.text: Lie beside the fire and keep the cold off {him} through the night

effects.log: The wind comes off the pole all night and goes round you like a river round a rock, and the fire never gutters. In the morning {npc} is asleep against your shell with the drum on {his} chest, and you do not move until {he} wakes.

events.text: Home on your own stretch of river after decades away, and the ferry people are three generations on and think you are a new tortoise. In the long nights you still see it: the bench of seven dark stars over the pole, and the space in the middle. The snake has stopped asking who sat there. It has started asking who will.

choices.text: The tortoise: say nothing, and go on looking north every clear night

effects.log: Every clear night for a century you lie on the ice of the ford facing north. The ferry people decide it is a sign of good fishing. It is not, but the fishing is good anyway.

choices.text: The snake: "Nobody, if they have any sense. It is cold up there"

effects.log: The snake says it, and then says it again a month later, and then again, and the tortoise notices that a creature who means a thing does not have to say it so often.

choices.text: Both heads: "Somebody slow, and somebody who counts"

effects.log: You say it together, without planning to, the way you sometimes finish each other's sentences now. Then you both go very quiet, because it sounded like a promise.

events.text: A warm winter, the second in a row. The river below the capital has not frozen, and the royal ice houses stand empty: no ice for the ancestral rites, none for the sick in summer, none to keep the dead cool for their funerals. So the court does what the old books say. At the riverside altar of the god who governs cold, an official in black robes sacrifices a black ox and offers bowls of black millet, and prays for the cold to come. Nobody comes. The official waits all night in the drizzle. You are under the river, and you are cold, and you find that you could answer.

choices.text: The tortoise: answer. Lie under the ford and breathe the cold out of you all night

effects.log: The drizzle turns to sleet and the sleet to snow, and before dawn the river locks from bank to bank. The official goes home soaked and astonished. The snake asks, quietly, who exactly the court thinks it was praying to.

choices.text: The snake: wait three nights until they are desperate, then answer

effects.log: On the third night the official has stopped praying and started weeping. Then the frost comes down like a lid. The whole court hears about the third night. The snake calls it good theatre; the tortoise calls it three nights of a man in the rain.

choices.text: Leave it. Winters are not yours to give, not yet

effects.log: The river stays open all winter. In summer the court has no ice and the sick lie in the heat. The snake says nothing at all, and you lie awake under the warm water hearing it say it.

events.text: The ice cutters go out on the river at night: men of the five wards of the capital, called up for it every winter, with long saws and iron picks and ropes. They cut blocks a hand thick and longer than a man and slide them over the ice to the ox-carts. The overseer has a whip and a lantern. A boy on the crew, too young for it, steps back from a block and through the edge of a hole into the black water.

choices.text: Come up under the boy and lift him on your back to the edge

effects.log: The boy comes up out of the hole on something black and broad and very cold, and is hauled out by his collar. He tells everyone he stood on the river god's back. The overseer whips him for lying. The crew does not believe the overseer.

choices.text: The tortoise: keep the ice thick under the whole crew all night, so nobody else goes in

effects.log: The boy is pulled out by his friends, blue but breathing. For the rest of the winter the ice under that crew is the thickest on the river, and they cut more blocks than any ward has ever cut, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: The snake: crack the ice under the overseer, just a little

effects.log: The overseer goes in to the waist, lantern and whip and all, and is pulled out by the same men he whipped. He is less free with the whip after that. The tortoise points out that the boy is still in the water, and the snake, a little ashamed, helps.

events.text: {npc}, keeper of the western ice house, comes down to the river alone at night with a cup of black millet wine. {His} family has kept the ice for four generations: the stacking, the straw, the ice tablets that tell each official how much ice each rank may have. "Something answered," {npc} says to the water. "My grandfather said once it did. I would like to thank it properly."

choices.text: The snake: put its head up out of the water and say thank you back

mem.note: spoke to me from the cold in the river

effects.log: {npc} does not drop the cup, which the snake respects. {He} pours it on the water instead, slowly, and bows, and from then on {his} family pours one cup every winter before the cutting.

choices.text: The tortoise: stay under and only let the cup go cold in {his} hands, as an answer

effects.log: The wine freezes in the cup. {npc} looks at it for a long time, then bows to the river and goes home with a frozen cup in both hands, the way people carry a relic.

choices.text: Ask {him}, through the snake, what the ice is for

effects.log: "The east house is for the rites," {npc} says. "The west house is for the officials, by rank. And in the worst of summer, for the old, and for the sick at the relief hospital, and for the prisoners, so they do not die of the heat." The tortoise asks which part matters. "The last part," {npc} says. "Always."

events.text: A fever summer, years later. The relief hospital outside the city gate is full and the west ice house is almost empty: the winter was thin again. {npc} comes to the river in the heat of the day, against every rule of {his} office, and stands in the shallows in {his} official robes. "There are forty in the hospital," {he} says. "I have ice for nine days."

choices.text: Go up the drainage channel and lie down under the ice house all summer

effects.log: You lie in the dark under the stone floor of the ice house through the whole summer, breathing out winter, and the last blocks do not melt. The forty live, most of them. You come out in autumn thin and dry and aching, and {npc} sits by the channel every evening until you are back in the river. (-12 health)

choices.text: Freeze the deep well in the hospital yard instead, from below

effects.log: The hospital well grows a skin of ice in the seventh month. The physicians do not ask why. They break it every morning with a pole and carry the ice to the beds.

choices.text: The snake: "Summer is the south's. We do not go where we are not seated"

effects.log: The snake is not wrong. {npc} goes home and the hospital buries eleven that summer. The tortoise does not argue, and the snake can feel it not arguing all the way to autumn.

events.text: You think about it under the ice, the way a tortoise thinks about anything: for years. A kingdom whose winters fail. A stone house half underground, packed with straw. The old and the sick in the heat. You could do more than answer a rite now and then. You could lie down under that house and not get up, and the king would have ice every summer, and nobody would know why.

choices.text: The tortoise: "Not yet. But I will remember the way there"

effects.log: You do not go. But you learn the drainage channel by heart, every turn of it, and you know you will be able to find it in the dark in a thousand years.

choices.text: The snake: "Never. A whole life under a storehouse, for people who do not know our name"

effects.log: The tortoise does not answer, and does not need to. The snake knows exactly which part of the sentence the tortoise disagreed with. It was the last part.

choices.text: Both heads: promise the keeper's family, in both voices, that the ice will not fail while you live

effects.log: The snake makes the promise and the tortoise means it. The keeper's family writes it on a board and hangs it in the ice house, where the officials think it is a charm. It is a contract.

events.text: Generations later, on a night of hard frost, you watch the ice cutters go out onto the river. Before the first saw goes in, the oldest of them kneels and pours a cup of black millet wine into a hole in the ice. None of them remembers why. It is just what you do, before the cutting.

choices.text: Let the cup reach you, and make the ice good this year

effects.log: The ice is clear and thick as a door all the way across. The cutters say it is the best year in living memory. It is a custom, they say. Customs work.

choices.text: The snake: breathe in its smell. Somebody should

effects.log: Black millet wine, a little sour, very cold, by the smell of it. The snake says it is the first offering it has ever had that smelled of anything. The tortoise lets it keep the whole cup, and pours it back into the river after.

events.text: The first frost of the year, and you wish, idly, the way you have wished every autumn for four hundred years, that the river would freeze tonight. It freezes. From your feet outward, in a white line, bank to bank, while the ferry is still tied up mid-stream with a cart on it. The ferryman stands on his deck looking at the ice, then at the water where you are, then at the ice again. Winter does not only listen to you now. It does what you ask.

choices.text: The tortoise: let it go slowly back to water by morning, and be careful what you wish from now on

effects.log: The ice thins and breaks up before dawn and the ferry gets across. You spend the next ten years wishing very small things very quietly, like someone carrying a full bowl.

choices.text: The snake: try it again tomorrow, further downstream, to see how far it goes

effects.log: Three villages downstream wake to a frozen river in the ninth month. Two of them hold a rite. The third moves its fish-weirs. The snake has found where the edge is: there isn't one.

choices.text: Both heads: freeze it once more, gently, so the ferryman can walk the cart to the bank

effects.log: The ice firms under the ferry just long enough for the cart to be led off. The ferryman leaves a bowl of millet on the bank and says nothing to anybody, which is the right thing to say.

events.text: A valley upriver has had three bad harvests, and the winter will not end. It is the third month and there is still snow in the paddies, and the people are boiling pine bark. An old woman of the valley walks down to the river with a bowl of the bark broth and pours it in. "Whoever keeps the winter," she says, "please. We have nothing left to offer but this."

choices.text: Shorten the winter by nine days. Nine days is a sowing

effects.log: The thaw comes nine days early and the valley sows in the mud before the frost can come back. Nine days is a harvest. The valley will not starve this year.

choices.text: The snake: "Who pays for the nine days?" Ask before you give them

effects.log: The winter you cut short has to go somewhere. The snake finds out: a late frost on the plum blossom in the next province, a poor fruit year there. You give the nine days anyway, but now you know the price, and the snake will not let you forget it.

events.text: A county magistrate has timber to send to the capital as tribute, and no money for rafts. He stands on the bank with a shaman and a drum, asking the river god to freeze the river by the tenth month so the logs can be dragged on sledges. The raftsmen of the county stand behind him with their arms folded. If the river freezes early, they will have no work this year.

choices.text: Freeze it. Tribute is tribute, and sledges are cheaper

effects.log: The river freezes in the tenth month and the logs go down it on sledges, pulled by the raftsmen at half a raftsman's wage. The magistrate is promoted. The snake asks who pays. This time it does not need to.

choices.text: The tortoise: keep the river open until its proper day

effects.log: The shaman drums for three days and the river runs on, black and indifferent. The raftsmen get their season. The magistrate tells the capital the river god is corrupt, which, as the snake points out, is a little rich.

events.text: A walled town on the river is under siege. On three sides it has walls; on the fourth, the river is its wall, wide and fast. The besiegers' general has heard that the river freezes when the north water's tortoise wishes it, and he has sent a black ox into the water at dawn with a prayer tied to its horns. If the river freezes, they will walk in over the ice.

choices.text: The tortoise: let the ox drown and the river run

effects.log: The siege lasts another winter and then breaks, as sieges do. The townspeople never know that the river was asked. The snake says the ox should be counted as a casualty. You count it.

choices.text: The snake: freeze a thin skin on the river, just thick enough to look solid

effects.log: The vanguard walks out onto ice that will hold a fox and not a man. The tortoise watches with both eyes shut, which is not possible, and it manages anyway. The siege is lifted in a morning. Nobody in either army forgets that river.

events.text: A wedding procession on the near bank: a bride in a red skirt and a green jacket in a palanquin, the groom's family waiting in the village across the river. The ice is breaking up a week early this year, grinding and groaning, and the ferry cannot cross through it. The bride's mother is weeping. The bride is not. She looks at the river as if it owed her something.

choices.text: Hold the ice one more week, thick as a road, for the procession

effects.log: The procession crosses on ice that should not be there, the palanquin swaying, the drums going, the bride looking straight ahead. Halfway over she leans out and drops a red date onto the ice, for whoever is holding it. The snake eats it.

choices.text: The tortoise: carry the palanquin across on your back, through the broken ice

effects.log: Eight bearers, a palanquin and a bride on a black shell, through grinding ice floes, while the drummers on the bank forget to drum. In that village they still tell it at every wedding. (-6 health)

events.text: Children on the river ice with sleds made of planks and a pair of iron skates their grandfather forged. One of them has gone too far out, toward the dark water at the bend where the current never lets it freeze, and is looking down into it, fascinated. Down there, looking back up, are two heads.

choices.text: Freeze the bend for the first time in a hundred years, under the child's feet

effects.log: The black water at the bend goes white in one breath. The child stands on it, astonished, then turns and runs back to the others to tell them, and none of them believe a word of it.

choices.text: The snake: hiss once, very loudly. Children learn from that

effects.log: The child goes back across the ice faster than a sled. Every child in that village is told from then on that the bend has a black snake in it. It does. It is the safest bend on the river.

events.text: Another winter, another petition. Someone on the bank wants the river frozen, or open, or the snow kept off a pass, or brought down on one. You can do it now without trying, and that is the trouble. The snake, as it does every time, asks the only question it has ever thought worth asking about winter: who pays.

choices.text: Grant it, and pay attention to who pays

effects.log: You give the winter they asked for and spend the rest of the year finding out who paid for it. It is never who you expected. The snake keeps the list.

choices.text: Refuse it, and let the year be what it would have been

effects.log: The year is what it would have been. Some people are worse off for your refusal, and you will never know their names. That is what refusing costs.

events.text: Black flags on the north bank: the black of the north, the old colour of the direction, flown by an army that has marched three hundred li in the snow. Its general, {npc}, comes down to the water alone in the dark and kneels. "They burned my villages in the autumn," {he} says to the river. "Their fortress is two days south. If I cross tonight I can take it before their reinforcements come. The stories say the tortoise of the north water freezes rivers for black flags." On your side of the river, the south bank, are four villages that have burned nothing.

choices.text: The tortoise: freeze it by dawn. The north asked

effects.log: The river locks under you, groaning, hour by hour. At dawn {npc} stands up, stiff with cold, and looks at the white road across the water, and does not thank you. {He} looks frightened, which is wiser.

choices.text: Keep it open. Break the ice all night if you must

effects.log: The cold comes down from the north whether you like it or not, and all night you break the ice as it forms, with your shell, from below, like a bell ringing under the river. At dawn the water is still black. {npc} stares at it a long time. (-6 health)

choices.text: The snake speaks: "Swear the south bank villages are spared, and the river is yours"

mem.note: swore an oath to the snake in the river

effects.log: {npc} swears on {his} ancestors, and on the black flag, with the snake's head a hand's width from {his} face. The river freezes. The tortoise notes that an oath is only a word kept, and wonders who will keep this one.

choices.text: Both heads: freeze it for the army's crossing only, and thaw it the moment the last horse is over

effects.log: The snake tells {npc} the terms and the tortoise holds them: one crossing, one morning, and then the river is a river again, with no road back. {npc} understands. An army that cannot retreat does not loot on its way.

events.text: The crossing. Five thousand men and two thousand horses on ice you made, in a column a li long, black flags dripping. The ice groans under them the whole way, and you lie under the middle of it with every plate of your shell feeling the weight. Halfway over, a supply wagon breaks through and goes down with its oxen.

choices.text: The tortoise: hold the ice thick under the column, whatever it costs

effects.log: You hold it. The wagon is lost and the oxen with it, but no man goes in. When the last horse steps onto the south bank you let go all at once, and lie in the dark water shaking for a month. (-12 health)

choices.text: The snake: bring the oxen up, at least

effects.log: The snake goes down after the wagon and comes up under the oxen, one by one, and the drovers haul them out over the edge of the hole screaming about river spirits. The tortoise holds the ice alone the whole time, and says afterwards that it did not mind, in a voice that minded. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let the ice thin under the rearguard, so the column cannot come back the same way

effects.log: The rearguard crosses on ice that sags under them like wet paper. They make it, just. The river opens behind them. Now nobody in that army can go home except through the fortress. The tortoise wanted a crossing, not a trap, and says so, once.

events.text: The river stays open. The black-flag army camps on the north bank for a month, then two. Their shamans beat drums at the water every night; they cut a hole and throw in a black ox; they throw in another. The men eat their horses. You lie under the open water and listen to an army starve, and {npc} comes down every evening and looks at the river without saying anything.

choices.text: The tortoise: keep the river open until they go home

effects.log: In the third month the black flags go north again, fewer than came. The four villages on the south bank never know how close it was. {npc} is the last to leave the bank, and bows to the water before {he} goes, which you did not expect.

choices.text: The snake speaks to {npc} at last: "Go home. The south will not cross either, while I keep this river"

effects.log: "Then it is a border," {npc} says slowly. "Not a road." {He} takes the army home. For a hundred years after, the river is a line neither side crosses, kept by something both sides are afraid of. A strange sort of peace. Peace, though.

events.text: Years later, the campaign ends, the way campaigns do, not with a battle but with a camp being struck. The army's winter quarters on the riverbank, the earth ramparts, the granary pits, the palisade of sharpened logs: all abandoned in a single week, the logs pulled up for firewood, the ramparts left to the snow. An army's works, ending. It belongs to the Encampment, the sixth mansion of the north, and you are here.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch every log come down, and write the Encampment plate true

effects.log: You watch from the shallows for seven days until the last cart is gone and the snow begins to fill the granary pits. Then you write it, slowly, in the grain of the plate: what you saw, and nothing you did not. The Encampment plate.

choices.text: The snake: write it now, from the first day, and go home; the rest is obvious

effects.log: The snake writes it quick and neat from the first day's packing: the Encampment plate, written, not quite true. On the fourth day, after you have gone, the camp catches fire. The plate does not know that. It cracks in the first frost.

choices.text: Watch it to the end anyway; the plate is already written, but the watching is not

effects.log: There is no plate for this one; your back already holds an Encampment. You watch anyway, every log, because something should. The snake watches with you and does not count, for once.

choices.text: Go home before it ends. You have seen enough armies

effects.log: You go back down the river. The camp ends without you. Somewhere a plate stays bare, and you find you can bear it.

events.text: {npc} comes back to the river alone, old, in a plain cotton coat with no flag. "I kept the oath," {he} says to the water. "The four villages. Nobody touched them. My own captains thought I was mad. I have come to ask the snake whether it knew I would."

choices.text: The snake: "No. That is why I asked you to swear"

effects.log: {npc} laughs until {he} coughs. "Good," {he} says. "I would have hated to be predictable." {He} sits on the bank until dark, and leaves a black flag folded on the stones, which the river takes.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "We knew you would keep it, or we would have written it down"

effects.log: {npc} does not quite understand, and nods anyway. The tortoise does not explain that on its back there is a plate for every ending it has ever seen, and that an oath kept is an ending too.

events.text: Every winter since the crossing, when the river freezes at the ford, the children of the four villages find something in the ice: a scrap of black cloth, frozen in, with a tortoise and a snake stitched on it in grey thread. It is never the same scrap. Nobody knows where they come from. They have started calling the ford the Black Flag Crossing.

choices.text: Let them keep finding them. It is a good story for a ford

effects.log: The children take the scraps home and their grandmothers sew them into padded jackets for luck. In a century there is not a child in the four villages without a black patch somewhere.

choices.text: The tortoise: bury the old flag deep in the riverbed, where the ice cannot bring it up

effects.log: The scraps stop. The name stays. Some things should be remembered without being kept, the tortoise says, and the snake says that is the most tortoise sentence it has ever heard.

events.text: The snake reads the ice on a winter morning and goes very still. "Books," it says. "A hall of them. Burning. Fifteen years, perhaps twenty. In the capital." It is the seventh mansion, the Wall: writing, and heaven's secret archive of books. The tortoise is already turning south.

choices.text: The tortoise: go now, and wait in the moat under the archive for as long as it takes

effects.log: You go down to the capital the slow way and settle into the moat beneath the archive wall, among the lotus roots and the old coins. The snake says fifteen years is a long time to wait for a fire. The tortoise says it is a short time to wait for anything.

choices.text: The snake: "We could write it from here, when it happens. The river will tell us"

effects.log: The tortoise does not answer, and does not go. That is an answer too. You stay on your river and the years pass, and the snake keeps one eye on the south.

choices.text: Both heads: go, and the snake will read every title on the shelves while the tortoise waits

effects.log: You settle in the moat together. The snake starts reading the spines through the barred windows of the archive on the very first night, and keeps a list. The tortoise keeps the snake.

events.text: Every few autumns the archive airs its books: the chests carried out into the courtyard, the volumes opened on racks in the sun against mould and bookworm, turned page by page by clerks with fans. {npc}, the youngest clerk, eats lunch on the edge of the moat and drops the crusts to the black thing in the water. {He} talks to it, the way people talk to fish. "The annals," {he} says. "Every day of every king. If these burned there would be no past at all."

choices.text: The snake: answer {him}, very quietly: "Then do not let them burn"

mem.note: told me from the moat not to let the books burn

effects.log: {npc} drops the whole rice ball in the moat and stares. Then, being a clerk, {he} goes and checks the fire buckets. All of them. Every week for years.

choices.text: The tortoise: say nothing. Be a stone in the moat, and listen

effects.log: You listen to {npc} for years: which king was cruel, which was only tired, which chronicle has the best handwriting. {He} never knows {he} is talking to a witness. {He} is talking to a witness.

events.text: War comes to the capital the way the snake read it would: in a hot dry spring, from the south road, faster than anyone believed. The palace burns the first night. The archive burns the second. You are in the moat, and the pages come down onto the water like black snow, still glowing. {npc} comes out of the smoke with a chest of the annals on {his} back and an old monk beside {him} with another, both coughing, both heading for the water gate.

choices.text: Carry the clerk's chest out through the water gate on your back, and the monk's

mem.note: carried the annals out through the moat

effects.log: Two chests of the annals go out of the burning city on a black shell, under the water gate, down the river, into the mountains. You do not see the archive end. You saved the part of it that mattered. There is no plate for that. (-15 health)

choices.text: The tortoise: stay in the moat and watch every page burn, and remember every title

effects.log: You watch the whole night. {npc} gets to the water gate with the chest, or does not; you do not look away from the archive to see. By morning there is nothing but the stone plinth and the smell. You write it true: the Wall plate, with every title you could read in the firelight.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake carries the clerk out while the tortoise stays and watches the rest

mem.note: carried me out through the moat

effects.log: The snake unwinds three coils, which it has never done, and drags the chest and the clerk to the water gate while the tortoise holds still in the moat and watches the archive end. It is the hardest thing you have ever done together. The Wall plate is true, and two chests are in the mountains. (-20 health)

events.text: News comes up the river the way all news does: a burned page caught in a weir, then a boatman's rumour, then a refugee family. The capital fell. The archive burned, the whole hall, every book. Exactly when the snake said. You were not there. "I can write it," the snake says. "From what the river says. It would count."

choices.text: The snake: write it, quick and neat, from the river's account

effects.log: The Wall plate, written from a boatman's rumour and a burned page: a hall of books, a night of fire. It is mostly true. The part that is not is the part nobody on the river knew: who carried what out, and who did not. The plate cracks in the first frost.

choices.text: The tortoise: go there now, however late, and see the ashes for yourself

effects.log: You get there two years after the fire. Weeds in the plinth, a stone lion with no head, a child selling scorched pages as kindling. It is not an ending you witnessed. It is what an ending leaves. You do not write it, yet. (-6 health)

choices.text: Leave it unwritten. Some endings were not yours to see

effects.log: The plate stays bare. The snake sulks for a decade. The tortoise does not mind the bare plate nearly as much as it would have minded a wrong one.

events.text: In a temple high in the mountains, in a hall with no windows, the annals that came out of the fire lie in chests on wooden racks, and a monk airs them every autumn. {npc}, grey now, comes every autumn to help. {He} finds you, one year, in the temple's stone cistern, where you are certainly too big to have got in. "I wondered when you would come to see them," {npc} says.

choices.text: The snake: ask {him} to read you one king's reign, any one

effects.log: {npc} reads all afternoon: an unremarkable king, a good harvest, a quarrel about a bridge, a comet. The snake listens to every word. The tortoise falls asleep and does not miss anything; it was there for most of it.

choices.text: The tortoise: just look at the chests a long time, and go

effects.log: You look at them the way you would look at eggs. {npc} understands, and leaves you alone with them until dark.

events.text: Long after the fire, on clear nights, you find yourself saying the titles of the burned books. The snake says them with you. You never read most of them; you saw a few spines, or caught a burning page as it fell, or came after and found only ash. It is not much of an archive. It is the only one some of those books have left.

choices.text: Say the whole list every winter, so it does not fade

effects.log: Three hundred and eleven titles, every winter, under the ice. Heaven's secret archive of books, the Wall is called in the old star books. Some of it is under your shell.

choices.text: The snake: make up the first lines of the ones nobody read

effects.log: The snake is very good at first lines. The tortoise listens with deep disapproval and a certain amount of enjoyment, and makes the snake promise never to tell anyone they are real.

events.text: A scholar of a much later dynasty walks the river bank with a servant, complaining. A great book was lost when the old capital burned, the chronicle of a whole century, and there is a gap in the history like a missing tooth. "Not even the first line survives," the scholar says. "Nobody alive has read a word of it." The snake has read the first line. It saw the page fall burning into the moat.

choices.text: The snake: say it, from the water, and let the scholar run

effects.log: The scholar does not run. The scholar sits down in the mud and writes it on a sleeve with a brush that is not wet. One line. It goes into the history, with a note: received from the river. Nobody believes the note.

choices.text: The tortoise: say nothing. One true line is not a chronicle

effects.log: The scholar goes on down the bank, complaining. You keep the line. The gap stays a gap, honestly. The snake calls this hoarding. The tortoise calls it not pretending.

events.text: Carvers come up the river from the south with measuring cords and charcoal and a letter with a royal seal. The prisoner of long ago, the envoy who sat by the well in the northern prison and escaped by the rabbit's trick, went home and became a king, and now the king is dead. The king's son wants the finest turtle in the land for the base of the old king's stele. "The old king told us, in the last years," says the head carver, {npc}, "that a black tortoise in a northern well once told the king the end of a story. We were told to find it, and measure it."

choices.text: The tortoise: come out onto the bank and let them measure every plate

effects.log: It takes the carvers a week: cords across the shell, charcoal rubbings of every plate, the snake measured separately and with great suspicion. {npc} sits up every night redrawing the head. "It is smiling," {he} keeps saying. "Why is it smiling?"

choices.text: The snake: "Measure us. In return, we choose a line of the inscription"

effects.log: {npc} cannot promise any such thing, and promises it, the way carvers do. The snake is satisfied. The tortoise thinks the snake has just bargained for something it does not yet know how to want.

choices.text: Go into the shell on the riverbank and be a rock

effects.log: "Perfect," says {npc}, measuring a shut shell on the bank. "It is already stone. It will be easy." The snake, inside, takes offence at this for a decade.

events.text: {npc}'s drawings are spread on the bank under stones: the turtle striding forward, its neck raised high, its legs stretched out, honeycomb hexagons on the shell, and a face that is very nearly laughing. The king's son wants it fierce. {npc} wants it cheerful, "because the old king was cheerful, even in prison". And the snake wants to be on it. "A stele turtle has no snake," says {npc}. "There is a dragon capstone on top."

choices.text: The tortoise: hold your head up and cheerful for a whole season, so {he} can get it right

effects.log: You hold a cheerful face for three months, which is longer than any tortoise has ever held one. {npc} carves the head from it. The king's son, who wanted fierce, looks at it once and stops arguing.

choices.text: The snake: "Then carve the capstone dragons coiled the way I coil"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the snake for a long time, then at the capstone drawing, then rubs out six dragons and draws them again, entwined, three to a side, round a pearl. "Hornless," {he} says. "Snakes with ideas." The snake has never been so pleased.

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise sits for the base and the snake sits for the capstone

effects.log: So the stele has both of you after all, a turtle striding below and serpents coiled above, with the old king's words in between. Nobody will ever know it is one creature. That suits you both.

events.text: The inscription is being cut. The heading is in the king's second son's own hand, raised characters, very fine: the stele of the great king. Below it, the deeds. {npc} brings you a rubbing to look at, wet from the stone. The prisoner in the north is there, one line, and the escape, one line. The well is not. The rabbit is not.

choices.text: The snake: insist on its line. The well, the rabbit, all of it

effects.log: {npc} cuts it at the very bottom, very small, where only someone lying on the grass would read it: in the north, in a well, the turtle told the rest. The second son never notices. It is the only line on the stele that is entirely true.

choices.text: The tortoise: "Leave it out. The king told the story; we only finished it"

effects.log: {npc} nods, relieved, and cuts the deeds as the court wrote them. The snake wanted its line. It does not get it. It sulks for a season, and then admits the inscription reads better without a rabbit.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to cut the king's cheerfulness into it somewhere, even one word

effects.log: {npc} finds a place: the king laughed in prison. Three characters. They are the ones that wear away first, centuries later, because everyone who reads the stele touches them.

events.text: The stele stands before the royal tomb in the green grass of the south: a stone turtle striding, head high, cheerful, a slab of words on its back, coiled serpents above. You come to see it at night, down three rivers and over a field. It looks like you. Stranger than that: lying beside it in the dark, you feel how it would be to lie down under it and not get up, and carry the words for ever.

choices.text: The tortoise: promise the stone that you will come back, when the stele falls

effects.log: You say it to the stone turtle under your breath, the way you would say it to a sleeping friend. The stone does not answer. You know it heard.

choices.text: The snake: "A stone copy is enough. One of us in stone is plenty"

effects.log: The snake says it twice on the way home. The tortoise lets it. A creature who means a thing does not have to say it twice.

choices.text: Both heads: lie beside it until dawn, and promise in both voices

effects.log: At dawn the tomb keepers find two long tracks in the dew beside the stele, one broad and one thin, and no tracks leading away. They tell nobody. They put a bowl of water by the turtle's feet every morning after that.

events.text: A war, long after. Soldiers camp in the tomb field and pull the stele slab down for a hearthstone; it breaks in three. The stone turtle remains, striding, cheerful, with nothing on its back, and the dragon capstone lies in the grass beside it, coiled serpents round a pearl. Between them, where the words were, there is only air.

choices.text: Renew the promise. The words are gone; the turtle is not

effects.log: You lie beside the stone turtle one night in the trampled grass. The stele is lost. The turtle remains. You understand, finally, that this was always going to be the shape of it.

choices.text: The snake: read the broken slab where it lies, and remember the deeds

effects.log: Three pieces of slab in a soldiers' hearth, black with soot. The snake reads all of it, even the small line at the bottom, and keeps it. One more archive under your shell.

events.text: A coastal war. Raiders' ships come over the sea every spring, hundreds of them, and the coast burns. Your errands for the Dragon King bring you down to the southern bays, and in one of them, at low tide, {npc} finds you: a commander of the coast, in a dark armour coat, with a brush and a sheaf of paper. {He} sits down on a rock out of reach and draws you for an hour without a word. Then: "A covered back," {he} says. "No arrows can reach you. Nobody can board you. Show me how the head goes in."

choices.text: The tortoise: sit still for the drawing, all afternoon, and put the head in and out for {him}

effects.log: You put the head in and out forty times. {npc} draws it forty times. By sunset there is a sheaf of drawings on the rock and the tide is coming in, and neither of you has moved.

choices.text: The snake: strike at the brush, to see what {he} does

effects.log: {npc} does not flinch. {He} draws the snake, mid-strike, very fast and very well, and says: "Good. Something that comes out of the shell and bites. I will want that too."

choices.text: Both heads: show {him} how the shell closes, and how both heads come out of it at once

effects.log: The shell shuts like a door. Then both heads come out together, the slow one and the quick one, and {npc} drops the brush. {He} picks it up and draws for the rest of the day, and never once asks what you are.

events.text: {npc} comes back with a shipwright and a model the length of an arm: a fighting ship with a roof over it like a shell, oar ports along the sides. "They will try to board," {he} says. "They always board. They jump across with swords. If the roof is smooth, they will stand on it."

choices.text: The snake speaks: "Then put spikes on its back, and cover them with straw mats"

effects.log: {npc} and the shipwright look at each other. Then at the snake. Then the shipwright goes off to find a blacksmith. "The straw is the cruel part," the tortoise says. "Yes," says the snake, pleased.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "A back is for carrying. Make it strong, not sharp"

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, and plates the roof with iron, smooth and very strong. Later, after the first boarding, {he} adds the spikes anyway, and sends you a note to say so. The snake keeps the note.

events.text: The head. {npc} wants a dragon's head at the bow, because dragons frighten raiders. The snake hisses so hard it goes hoarse. "A turtle's head," says {npc} slowly, looking at you. "That goes in when the fighting is close, and comes out to breathe. And breathes what?" The snake breathes out over {his} lantern, a little winter, and the lantern smokes like a fog.

choices.text: The tortoise: put the head forth, slowly, and let {him} see how a turtle's head is made

effects.log: The head at the bow is carved from your head: a turtle's head, wide-mouthed, with a pipe in its throat to burn sulphur and saltpetre and pour out smoke like a sea fog over the enemy. It is a turtle's head. It is always going to be a turtle's head.

choices.text: The snake: "Smoke. Thick and yellow. They should not see you coming"

effects.log: {npc} burns sulphur in a pot for a week and nearly chokes {his} whole command. Then {he} gets it right: yellow fog out of the head's mouth, and the ship coming through it. The snake is insufferable for a decade.

choices.text: Let {him} have the dragon. Humans are frightened of the right things for the wrong reasons

effects.log: A dragon's head it is, carved and gilded. The snake does not speak to the tortoise for a season, and not to {npc} ever again.

events.text: The first battle. The covered ship goes into the raiders' fleet ahead of all the others, smoke pouring from its head, cannon firing from the ports on both sides, and the raiders try to board and find spikes under the straw. You are under the water beneath it. The ship turns too sharply in the current and heels over, and for a breath it could go either way.

choices.text: The tortoise: come up under the keel and hold it steady through the turn

effects.log: The keel comes down on your shell like a house falling and you hold it. The ship rights itself and goes on through the fleet, burning everything it passes. {npc} writes in a diary that night that the ship turned as if something under the sea had steadied it. (-12 health)

choices.text: The snake: cut the anchor ropes of the raiders' flagship, one by one

effects.log: The raiders' flagship drifts onto the rocks at the mouth of the bay, and the rest follow it in confusion. Nobody on either side ever knows why. The tortoise, watching the covered ship heel and right itself on its own, holds its breath the whole time.

choices.text: Stay down. This is a human war; let it be won by humans

effects.log: The ship rights itself on its own. The battle is won without you. You are prouder of that than of anything you could have done, and the snake, who wanted to help, says so with a great deal of feeling.

events.text: The last battle of the war, at night, in a strait full of fire. The raiders are going home and {npc} will not let them go easily. Toward dawn a stray shot finds {him} on the deck. {He} is carried below. Before the end {he} asks for the drawings, the first ones, of you at low tide, and tells an aide to throw them into the sea. "The tortoise should have them back," {npc} says. "Tell it to keep this coast."

choices.text: Take the drawings from the water, and keep this coast

effects.npcPass: a stray shot in the last battle of the war
effects.log: The drawings come down through the dark water to you, ink running, forty heads going in and out of a shell. You keep them under your plastron. You keep the coast too. Neither is easy.

choices.text: The snake: take them, and let the coast keep itself

effects.npcPass: a stray shot in the last battle of the war
effects.log: The snake keeps the drawings. The coast is not yours. The tortoise says nothing, and you both know that the tortoise has already promised, on its own, in the dark, and that the snake heard.

events.text: A scholar of a much later age, writing a history of the war, comes to the southern bay to look at the sea. You hear the scholar's servant read the draft aloud on the rocks: the covered ship, the iron roof, the spikes under straw, "and at the bow, a dragon's head, breathing smoke". The snake goes rigid with outrage.

choices.text: The snake: put its head out of the sea and say, very clearly, "Turtle"

effects.log: The servant drops the draft in a rock pool. The scholar picks it up, reads the wet line again, and crosses out dragon. Then, being a scholar, writes it back in the next morning, because all the other books say dragon.

choices.text: The tortoise: let it be. You were there. That is enough

effects.log: It was a turtle's head. You saw it carved from yours. The history will say what it says, and your back will say what it saw, and only one of them is true.

events.text: {npc}, a painter of the royal bureau, comes to your river with a servant, a folding easel and an order: a screen of the ten long-lived things for the New Year. The sun, clouds, mountains, rocks, water, the pine, the crane, the deer, the herb of long life, and the turtle. "Every painter copies the turtle from an older painter," {npc} says. "Nobody has seen one that has lived a thousand years. They say you have."

choices.text: The tortoise: sit for {him} on the rock by the ford, as long as {he} likes

effects.log: You sit for a whole autumn. {npc} paints you nine times and throws eight away. The ninth turtle has a little smile and a shell like an inkstone, and is the first turtle in that genre painted from life.

choices.text: The snake: "Paint me too, or paint nothing"

effects.log: {npc} is very sorry: the turtle in the screen has no snake, there is a model book. The snake argues for a week. In the end {npc} paints a long strand of waterweed trailing over the turtle's shell, black, with a suspicious head. Everyone is satisfied.

choices.text: Both heads: sit, and let the snake tell {him} about the other nine

effects.log: The snake knows the crane by name and the pine by age and the deer by its bad habits. {npc} paints from the snake's descriptions and from the tortoise's stillness, and the screen comes out stranger and better than the model book.

events.text: The crane in the screen is real too: an old crane in the pine above the painter's easel, red-capped, standing on one leg, looking down at you with great condescension. "The turtle," it says, "is always in the corner. Low down, by the water, under the important things. Filling a space." It has been in the pine for nine hundred years and has opinions about everything.

choices.text: The snake: "And the crane is always in the sky, being decorative"

effects.log: The crane is so offended it nearly falls out of the pine. It is the beginning of a friendship, though neither of you will call it that for a very long time.

choices.text: The tortoise: "Someone has to hold up the corner"

effects.log: The crane opens its beak to answer and finds it has nothing to say, which has not happened to it since the time of the first kings. It flies off in a huff and is back the next morning.

events.text: A white deer comes down to the stream at dusk to eat the herb of long life, which grows only on the rocks above your ford. It eats one leaf, slowly, and looks at you over it. It has lived a thousand years, it says, by never fighting anything: when the hunters come, it is somewhere else. The snake finds this unbearable.

choices.text: The snake: argue with it about running away

effects.log: The argument lasts nine years. The deer wins it by not being there whenever the snake has thought of a good answer. The snake has never been so angry with anything that did not try to eat it.

choices.text: The tortoise: understand it. Hiding is not running away

effects.log: You and the deer understand each other perfectly, in silence, every dusk for a century. The snake calls you both cowards. The deer says that is exactly the point.

events.text: The old pine on the rock above the ford, the one the painter painted, has been in every screen in that bureau for six hundred years. It speaks, if you wait. You ask it a question one spring, and the answer begins to arrive eleven years later, one word every autumn when the wind is right.

choices.text: The tortoise: wait for the whole answer, however long it takes

effects.log: The answer takes forty years. It is: roots go down as far as branches go up. The snake has long since forgotten the question. The tortoise thinks it was worth every year, and so, eventually, does the snake.

choices.text: The snake: guess the end of the sentence and save forty years

effects.log: The snake guesses wrong, of course, and the pine, offended, stops talking for a century. The tortoise waits for it anyway. It is that sort of tortoise.

events.text: The screen goes up in the palace for the New Year: ten long-lived things on twelve panels, gold and green and deep blue, and in the corner by the water, low down, under the important things, a turtle with a little smile and a black strand of waterweed with a suspicious head. A minister at a sixtieth birthday is given a copy. Then another. Then every painter in the bureau copies it from {npc}'s, and the turtle in the corner is you, for ever.

choices.text: Let it be. A corner is a good place to hold up

effects.log: Three hundred years of New Years, and in every palace and every rich house, you in the corner, holding it up. The crane is furious that its copies are no better than everyone else's.

choices.text: The snake: count the copies, every one, for as long as there are copies

effects.log: The snake loses count at four thousand and starts again. Every one of them has the waterweed now. The model books have changed. The snake has never been happier.

events.text: The crane from the pine comes down onto the ice one winter, very formally, and makes an announcement: it will outlive you. It has a thousand years, it says. You have a thousand years, the snake says. It has more, says the crane. Whoever is left, it proposes, must write the other's ending. The tortoise thinks this is the most sensible suggestion it has heard from a bird.

choices.text: The tortoise: agree, and mean it

effects.log: You agree. The crane is slightly put out that you were not more frightened. It had a speech ready.

choices.text: The snake: agree, and add that the crane's ending will be very short

effects.log: "Crane. Flew about. Stood on one leg. Died." The snake recites it every spring from then on, to keep in practice. The crane pretends not to hear, and stands on the other leg.

events.text: The crane is dying. It says so, lying on the bank with its wings spread out and its eyes shut. It says so for two days, in detail, and asks whether you have your brush ready. On the third day it stands up, shakes itself, and flies off. It was moulting.

choices.text: Write the first line of its ending anyway, for practice

effects.log: The snake writes it in the snow: the crane of the ford, who died of moulting. The crane comes back that evening, reads it, and does not speak to you for a year.

choices.text: The tortoise: say nothing, and be glad

effects.log: You are glad, and the crane can tell, and that embarrasses it far more than anything the snake could have said.

events.text: The crane is dying again. This time, the snake points out, it was this very week last time. The crane says that moulting at its age is a great deal like dying and it would thank you to show some respect. Then it asks, quietly, with its eyes shut, whether you would really write it. Truly. Not the snake's version.

choices.text: The tortoise: "Truly. Every leg you stood on"

effects.log: The crane opens one eye and shuts it again, satisfied. It recovers, of course. But from then on it is a different sort of bird around you: one who knows that someone will be there.

choices.text: Both heads: "Truly. And the snake will make it interesting"

effects.log: The crane laughs, which cranes are not built for, and nearly does die. You both spend the night keeping it warm. It was moulting.

events.text: This time it is real. The crane lies under the pine in the snow, very light, very old, and does not say anything at all, which is how you know. The snake, for once, has no ending ready. You stay with it through the night, and at dawn the pine drops a little snow on all three of you.

choices.text: Write it true, in full, every leg it stood on

effects.log: It takes the whole winter. Nine hundred years of standing on one leg in a pine, being decorative, being rude, being there. It is the longest ending you have ever written. It does not go on a plate. It goes under them, where you keep the things that matter.

choices.text: The snake: write the short version, as promised. Then the long one

effects.log: "Crane. Flew about. Stood on one leg. Died." And then, underneath, for a month, everything else. The snake does not recite it in spring any more.

events.text: The autumn equinox. You are lying in the deepest part of your water, where the old channels run away under the mountains to the east, when a green light comes down them like a lantern lowered into a well. A dragon: young, blue-green, whiskered, longer than your river is wide, diving from somewhere east, from the abyss under some ridge, the way every dragon dives when the year turns. It does not see you. It curls up in the dark below you, where it is warm, and goes to sleep. It is the most beautiful thing that has ever come into your water, and it has no idea where it is.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie across the mouth of the channel all winter, so nothing comes near it

effects.log: Eels, a drowned log, a curious otter: nothing gets past. The dark down there stays warm and wordless all winter. That is what it came for. It will never know that someone had to keep it so.

choices.text: The snake: go down and look at it closely. Count its claws

effects.log: Four claws, the snake reports, and a scar on the jaw, and it snores. The dragon stirs as the snake goes by, and mutters something about rain, and sleeps on. The snake comes back up full of it.

choices.text: Both heads: keep the dark warm and wordless for it; the snake does not count, for once

effects.log: The hardest part is the snake not counting. It manages. All winter the deep is silent as the inside of a shell, and the green light breathes in it, slow and easy. You have never kept anything so carefully that did not belong to you.

events.text: The spring equinox. Very faintly, through the rock and the water, from somewhere far to the east, you hear drums: children beating buk drums at the edge of a pool and singing a song you cannot make out. The green light below you does not move. The dragon is still asleep, and it is spring.

choices.text: Nudge it, gently, toward the channel and the drums

effects.log: The dragon wakes slowly, blinks, and goes up the channel toward the drums without a backward look. It thinks it woke on its own. Somewhere east, a pool boils, and children cheer.

choices.text: The snake: "It is young. Let it sleep one more week"

effects.log: It sleeps one more week, and rises late, and somewhere east the plum is late and the children drum all week. The snake says it was worth it. The tortoise says the children might not agree.

events.text: A winter when the green light is asleep below you, and something comes fishing for it. Through a hole in the ice above, a bronze mirror on a long iron chain comes down, turning slowly, with talismans tied along the links: a dragon-hunter monk, after horn and pearl, who has heard that dragons sleep in deep water in winter.

choices.text: The snake: bite through the chain

ok.log: The snake goes up the chain like a black flame and bites it through at the ice. The mirror goes down into the dark and the monk sits down hard on the ice holding a length of iron. The dragon sleeps through all of it.

fail.log: The chain is talisman-iron and the snake's teeth skid on it. The tortoise drags the whole length sideways into the rocks instead, and the monk loses it there. The snake's mouth aches all winter. (-10 health)

choices.text: The tortoise: let the mirror find you instead, and show it only a black shell

effects.log: The monk hauls up the mirror and looks into it and sees a black shell as big as a threshing floor, and nothing else. A thousand-year tortoise. Worth a fortune. The diviners will hear of it. The dragon will not.

choices.text: Draw the whole pool cold until the hole freezes shut over the chain

effects.log: The ice closes round the chain in an hour and holds it like a fist. The monk pulls until dusk and goes away. In spring the chain is still there, frozen into the ice, with a bronze mirror on the end that reflects only dark.

events.text: The dragon is older now, and it comes down at the equinox differently: hot, restless, the green of it with a harder shine. It does not sleep easily. It turns and turns in the dark below you, and the water round it is warm as a bath. You know nothing about dragons. You know a great deal about fevers that need cooling.

choices.text: The tortoise: breathe cold down into the deep all winter, slowly, until it sleeps

effects.log: The fever goes out of the water a little at a time. By midwinter the dragon lies still, and its light is soft again, and it sleeps like something that has put a heavy thing down. In spring it rises humbler than it came. It thinks the dark did that.

choices.text: The snake: let it toss. It came here to cool off on its own

effects.log: It tosses all winter and rises in spring still hot, and you hear later, through the river, that a valley in the east had a bad year of storms. The snake says that is not your business. The tortoise says everything that sleeps in your water is.

events.text: The dragon talks in its sleep. Not often; once a winter, perhaps. About a valley, and a well, and a tiger on the ridge across from it that quarrels about the rain. About a village called the Elbow. About a child who once asked it why the sky is blue. The snake lies very still and listens to every word.

choices.text: The snake: remember all of it. Secrets are worth keeping

effects.log: By spring the snake knows more about the dragon of the east than the dragon's own valley does. It does not use any of it. It keeps it the way it keeps everything: just in case.

choices.text: The tortoise: cover the snake's ears with the rim of the shell. It is the dragon's sleep

effects.log: The snake is furious, and goes on furious until spring. But the dragon's sleep stays its own. The tortoise thinks some things are not for writing down, and is not sure the snake will ever agree.

choices.text: Both heads: listen, and then agree to forget, together

effects.log: You hear it all. In spring, on the riverbed, you play stones and agree, move by move, to forget, and you nearly manage it. What is left is only that the dragon loves a valley, which you knew.

events.text: Deeper than the dragon usually goes, where the channels meet the water under the world, something else is asleep: grey, almost stone, older than any valley, with moss in its whiskers and fish living in its ears. It was asleep there when you came; you have never woken it. This winter the young dragon goes down to it, and wakes it, and they talk for a long time in the dark, and in spring the young dragon does not rise.

choices.text: The tortoise: open the channels so the children's drums come down clear to it

effects.log: Three springs it stays down. On the third, you open every channel from the eastern pool to the deep, and the drums come down through the rock like a heartbeat, and a song: come up, come up, the plum is out, the ox is hungry. On the fourth spring it rises. It thinks the children called it back. They did. You only made sure it heard.

choices.text: The snake: "It is its own life. Let it decide"

effects.log: You wait. It is the longest three springs of your life, and the tortoise does not sleep through one hour of them. In the end it rises on its own, slowly, toward the drums. The snake says: see. The tortoise says nothing, and does not let the snake see how much it had wanted to help.

events.text: The autumn equinox, and the green light comes down the channels again, as it has for years: a little longer this time, a little brighter, the same scar on the jaw. It curls up in the warm dark below you and is asleep before it has stopped moving. You settle across the mouth of the channel, the way you always do.

choices.text: Keep the deep quiet all winter, as always

effects.log: A quiet winter in the deep. The dragon sleeps. Nothing comes near. In spring it rises without looking back, and you do not mind. That is what keeping is.

choices.text: The snake: leave one small fish by its nose, for the morning

effects.log: In spring the dragon wakes with a fish beside its nose, eats it, and rises, puzzled and pleased. The snake does it every year after that. The dragon starts to expect it.

events.text: The first snow, and something arrives from the west. Not weather: a weight, a parcel of cold handed to you over a great distance, the way a cup is handed across a table. You know whose it is without being told. Somewhere in the western mountains a white tiger has gone into its den, and lain down, and given its winter to the Black Tortoise. To you. It does it every year. You have only now grown big enough to feel it land.
events.arc: The Tiger Who Gives You Winter

choices.text: The tortoise: hold it carefully all winter, and give it back whole in the spring

effects.log: You hold the western winter the way you would hold an egg, and in spring you let it go back west unbroken. Somewhere a tiger wakes hungry and rested, and does not know why it slept so well.

choices.text: The snake: open it a little and see what is inside a tiger's winter

effects.log: Inside: hunger, and a mountain god with a white beard, and ghosts. A great many ghosts, walking behind it in the snow. The snake shuts it again quickly and is quiet for a month.

choices.text: Both heads: hold it, and let the snake read only the top of it, like the outside of a letter

effects.log: The top of it is just: tired. A judge who has judged all autumn and wants to sleep. You keep it warm, in the cold way you keep things. In spring it goes back west feeling held.

events.text: The tiger's winter is heavier this year. It comes with things in it: the ghosts of the ones it ate, cold and lost, walking round and round in the white like oxen at a millstone. They cannot sleep. The tiger has given you its winter, and it has given you them with it, whether it meant to or not.
events.arc: The Tiger Who Gives You Winter

choices.text: The tortoise: lay them down in the cold, quietly, one by one, until spring

effects.log: Cold is good for that. By spring nine of them are asleep, deep in the winter, and do not go back west with it. The tiger will find its road a little lighter and never know why.

choices.text: The snake: ask each of them its name and its village, and keep the list

effects.log: Forty names, forty villages, forty roads where the tiger met them. The snake keeps the list. It is not sure what for. The tortoise thinks it knows: someday someone will read the tiger's record aloud, and the list will matter.

events.text: In the autumn, before the tiger's winter comes, you decide to send something back the other way: news of the north, so the tiger knows who it has been handing its winters to all these years. The snow geese are going south and west in long lines. One of them would carry a short word. Geese do not do long ones.
events.arc: The Tiger Who Gives You Winter

choices.text: Send a sprig of frost from the north sea, and nothing else

effects.log: The goose carries it west in its beak, a twig of white rime that should melt in a day and does not. Somewhere in the western mountains a white tiger finds it on the snow outside its den, and sniffs it a long time.

choices.text: The snake: send a word. "Slept well?"

effects.log: The goose that carries it is not one of your geese and nearly forgets it on the way. It arrives as "Slept?" The tiger, apparently, finds this very funny.

choices.text: The tortoise: send nothing. A gift should not ask for an answer

effects.log: You send nothing. The tiger's winter comes as always, and you hold it as always. Some friendships are kept by never mentioning them.

events.text: A magpie comes all the way north, which magpies do not do, and lands on the river ice beside you, ruffled and furious with the cold. In its beak is a single white hair as long as your neck. "From the west," it says. "The old one says: slept very well. Also: the winter you sent back last spring was folded wrong." It flies off before the snake can answer.
events.arc: The Tiger Who Gives You Winter

choices.text: Laugh, both heads at once

effects.log: You laugh out loud with both heads, which you have never done, and the ice cracks from bank to bank with the sound of it. The ferry people say the river god is in a good mood. It is.

choices.text: The tortoise: keep the white hair under your shell, with the important things

effects.log: It lies beside the other things you keep. The archive under your plates is getting crowded.

events.text: A plague of locusts in the south and west: the sky brown with them, the rice going under. A hard early frost would kill them in a night. You could bring it. But the harvest is the west's, the tiger's autumn, and if your frost comes before the rice is cut, half of it will die in the fields with the locusts.
events.arc: The Tiger Who Gives You Winter

choices.text: Send word west first, and wait for the tiger to bring the harvest forward

effects.log: The goose goes west. A week later, all over the land, the rice yellows at once, in one great breath, and the farmers are in the fields day and night. The last sheaf is in the barn the evening before your frost. You send one word west: "Neat."

choices.text: Bring the frost now. Locusts do not wait for courtesy

effects.log: The frost comes down in the night and the locusts die in drifts. So does half the rice. In the west, a tiger wakes in its den and growls at the north for a week. You hear it through the ground.

choices.text: The tortoise: wait. The tiger's autumn is the tiger's

effects.log: You wait until the rice is in. The locusts eat a third of it first. Nobody is happy, which is how the guardians show they have respected each other.

events.text: The snake reads it in the river ice, in a crack that runs from bank to bank in the shape of a roof ridge: a dynasty's end. Not a house, a whole house of kings. Sixty years from now, give or take, the great hall in the capital will burn and its roof will fall in, and the treasury will be empty under it. The Rooftop, the fifth mansion of the north. The tortoise is already turning toward the capital.

choices.text: The tortoise: go now, and wait in the palace pond for sixty years

effects.log: You go down to the capital and in through the water gate, and settle into the mud of the palace lotus pond among the carp. Sixty years. The tortoise has waited longer for less.

choices.text: The snake: "Sixty years. We could sleep fifty-five and then go"

effects.log: The tortoise goes now anyway, and the snake goes with it, because the snake goes where the tortoise goes. It says the pond is boring. It is right. It is also, the snake discovers, full of very fat carp.

events.text: The palace pond. Lotus in summer, ice in winter, carp who have been fed by kings for so long they will not eat anything else. And a child, the crown prince, {npc}, who comes to the pond every morning with a bowl of rice cakes and talks to the fish because nobody else in the palace will listen. One morning {he} sees you. "A turtle," {he} says, delighted. "A black one. That means long life."

choices.text: The tortoise: let the child see you every morning, and listen

mem.note: listened to me in the pond
