effects.log: Every morning for years {npc} tells you about tutors and ministers and a father who is always tired. You learn more about the dynasty from one lonely child than from all the omens in the ice.

choices.text: The snake: take the rice cakes and stay hidden. Do not get fond of it

effects.log: The snake eats the rice cakes and does not get fond of the child, every morning, for years, with great determination. The tortoise does not have to say anything about this, and doesn't.

events.text: {npc} is king now, young and tired, with the court split three ways and the granaries sold off by ministers who smile at {him}. The signs are everywhere, if you know the ice: a famine in the south, a rebel's name in every inn, a treasury that rings hollow. {npc} still comes to the pond at night, alone. "Is it bad?" {he} asks the water. "The fish do not know. Does the turtle?"

choices.text: The tortoise: say nothing. You came to witness, not to rule

effects.log: {npc} waits for an answer that does not come, and goes back up the steps. The snake does not speak to the tortoise for a week. It does not need to. The silence is a whole argument.

choices.text: The snake speaks: "Yes. Sell nothing more. Open the granaries in the south"

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the edge of the pond as if {his} legs had gone. Then {he} goes up and does it, half of it, against half the court. The tortoise was overruled, and says so in the only way it has: by not moving for a month.

events.text: The last night, as the snake read it, nearly to the year. Rebels at every gate. The guards have opened two of them. The great hall is burning from the eaves inward, the tiles falling into the courtyard like hail, and the treasury doors stand open on nothing. {npc} comes down to the pond in {his} robes with a sword {he} does not know how to use, and looks at the water.

choices.text: The tortoise: stay in the pond and watch it to the end, every beam, and write the Rooftop plate true

effects.npcPass: the last night of the dynasty, by the palace pond
effects.log: You watch until the roof ridge falls in and the sparks go up like a second sky. {npc} sits by the pond till the end. You do not look away. In the morning you write it, slowly: the Rooftop plate, true, with one child's rice cakes in it.

choices.text: Carry {npc} out through the water gate on your back. Let the dynasty end without its last king

effects.log: You carry a king out under the water gate and down the river to a fishing village where nobody knows {his} face, and {he} lives forty more years as a net-mender. The dynasty ends anyway. You were not there to see it. There is no plate. The tortoise lets the snake have this one, and minds. (-12 health)

choices.text: The snake: write it now, from the first sparks, and get the king out too

effects.log: The snake writes the Rooftop plate as the first beam catches, quick and neat, and then you go for the water gate with {npc} on your back. The plate says the king died in the hall. The king is mending nets downriver. It cracks in the first frost.

events.text: The year the snake read comes, and goes, and nothing burns. {npc} is an old king now, stooped, with a reign the chroniclers will call unremarkable, which is the best thing a chronicler can say. The granaries are full. The hall's roof was retiled last spring. The crack in the river ice that looked like a roof ridge has healed over. There is no ending here to write.

choices.text: The snake: be smug about it, at length

effects.npcPass: old age, in a reign that did not end in fire
effects.log: The snake is smug for a decade. The tortoise lets it be. There is a bare place on your back where a Rooftop plate would have been, and an old king who dies in bed, and the tortoise, which wanted to write, finds it does not want the plate as much as it wanted that.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie in the pond one more year, just to be sure

effects.npcPass: old age, in a reign that did not end in fire
effects.log: Nothing happens in that year either. The old king dies in the winter, in bed. You go home up the river with no plate and a lighter shell than you came with.

events.text: Years on, a new dynasty is building a new palace on the ruins of the old one. The workmen dig up the old roof tiles by the cartload: grey tiles with a lotus pattern on the round ends, scorched black. A child of one of the workmen brings one down to the pond to wash it, and finds the pond still has a turtle in it.

choices.text: The snake: tell the child what the tile saw

effects.log: The child listens with the tile in both hands. That child grows up to be a chronicler, which may be a coincidence. The snake says it is not.

choices.text: The tortoise: go home. The new roof is someone else's ending

effects.log: You go up the river. Behind you the new roof goes up, and someday it will come down, and a snake somewhere will read it in the ice. Not this one. Not this time.

events.text: In the palace pond, one winter, the snake says what it has been thinking for twenty years. "We could save it. Not by speaking. By an omen: the king believes in omens. I write a prophecy on your back, in the ink of your own shell; we get ourselves dug up in the garden; the shaman reads it; the king is frightened into sense." The tortoise has heard this story before. It was a turtle dug up in a palace garden with writing on its back, and the shaman who read it was killed, and the city fell that summer anyway. "We witness," the tortoise says. "That is all we are for."

choices.text: The snake wins: write the omen

effects.log: The tortoise does not agree. The tortoise is overruled. It holds still while the snake writes, because there is nowhere else for it to go, and that is the worst part.

choices.text: The tortoise wins: no omen. Wait, and witness

effects.log: The snake does not agree. The snake is overruled. It does not argue. It goes quiet, which in a snake is the beginning of something.

choices.text: Both heads: neither wins tonight. Argue it out on the bed of the pond, as long as it takes

effects.log: You argue all winter, in whispers, so the carp will not hear. Neither of you gives an inch. At least you are still talking. That, it turns out, is the whole difference.

events.text: A year when neither head speaks. You eat; you sleep; you lie in the mud of the pond; the snake goes out at night and comes back before dawn and does not say where. You have shared one body for centuries and never felt it so crowded. On the bed of the pond, the black and white pebbles you play stones with lie where you left them, mid-game.

choices.text: The tortoise: wait it out. A tortoise can wait longer than anything

effects.log: You wait. The snake waits too, and it turns out a snake can wait a long time when it is angry. A whole year passes. Waiting is not the same as mending, and you both know it by the end.

choices.text: The snake: unwind one coil, and lie beside the shell instead of round it

effects.log: In the night the snake unwinds one turn from your shell, and lies beside you instead, and does not explain. The tortoise feels the cold where it was, all winter.

choices.text: Go to the pebbles and make the next move, without a word

effects.log: One white pebble, pushed a finger's width with a claw. Nothing for a week. Then, in the night, a black one moves. Nobody says anything. The game goes on.

events.text: The snake writes. In the ink of your own shell, with its chin, on the broad plate over your spine, in characters the court will read: the roof falls in the year the granaries are sold; open them, and it stands. Then you dig into the bank of the palace garden and wait to be found. A gardener's spade rings on your shell in the spring. There is shouting. The court shaman is sent for.

choices.text: Let the shaman read it, and hope

ok.log: The shaman reads it to the king exactly as written. The king, who has been told he is doomed by every star-watcher in the bureau, is told for once how not to be. The granaries open. The roof stands. The snake has saved a dynasty with a lie that came true. The tortoise has no plate, and an ache in the back where the writing was.

fail.log: The shaman reads it truly, and the king has the shaman beaten to death for it, the way the old story goes. They throw you back in the river. The snake says nothing for a long time. Then it says: you were right. The tortoise would give a great deal not to have been. (-10 health)

choices.text: The tortoise, at the last moment: dig back down before the spade comes again

effects.log: You go down into the bank so deep the gardeners give up and decide it was a stone. The writing stays on your back, unread, and the snake does not speak to you until autumn. The roof will fall when it falls.

events.text: The snake has stopped arguing. That is worse. It eats when you eat and sleeps when you sleep and answers when spoken to, and lies very loose around the shell, two coils where there were three, and looks at the water gate of the palace pond the way a prisoner looks at a door. The Knot is not breaking. It is going slack.

choices.text: The tortoise: say it. "You might have been right"

effects.log: It costs the tortoise more than any journey it has ever made. The snake turns and looks at it, almost, out of the corner of one eye, which is as close as the two of you can come. Then it winds one coil back.

choices.text: Take the snake out of the pond, upriver, and let it choose a fight with something

effects.log: An otter twice its weight, on a bank three days upriver. The snake wins, and bleeds, and comes back to the shell almost cheerful. Sometimes a quarrel is just a snake that has been in a pond too long. (-8 health)

events.text: How you make up, in the end: not with words. One spring night, on the bed of the river, the black and white pebbles laid out between you, and a game played to the very last stone. The snake cheats twice. The tortoise lets it. You both know. When the game is over neither of you can say who won, and neither of you asks.

choices.text: Play another

effects.log: You play all spring. By summer the snake is wound three times round the shell again, tight, and the tortoise has not noticed it happening, which is how it should be.

choices.text: Both heads: say it at the same moment, the way you sometimes finish each other's sentences: "Next time, ask me first"

effects.log: It comes out as one sentence in two voices, and you both hear it, and are both so startled you laugh. That is the end of the quarrel, and the beginning of something you do not have a word for yet.

events.text: Long after the quarrel, the snake reads another omen in the ice: a bridge, a crossing, somewhere far downriver, twenty years out. And before the tortoise can turn toward it, the snake asks: "Go and wait? Or do I write it from here? You decide this time. I mean it."

choices.text: The tortoise: "We go. Both of us. And you read the water on the way"

effects.log: You go. It is the same slow journey it always is, and the snake reads every eddy on the way and tells the tortoise what each one means, and for once the tortoise listens to all of it.

choices.text: The tortoise: "You decide. You asked; that was the point"

effects.log: The snake is so surprised it decides to go and wait. It says it would have anyway. The tortoise says it knows.

events.text: Byeolju comes up the river after long years away, in the same black gauze hat, fraying now at the brim, the kelp scroll shaking in its flipper. It is very old. It bows three times, slowly. "The Dragon King is sick again," it says. "The physicians of the palace have read the old books. Last time it was a rabbit's liver. This time they say..." It stops. "They say a thousand-year shell, ground fine, in wine. I was told to bring you down. I was not told to tell you why."
events.arc: The Dragon King Is Sick Again

choices.text: Go down to the palace anyway. Byeolju should not go back alone

effects.log: You go down the river and into the sea beside the old turtle, slowly, the way two old officials walk to a meeting both know will go badly. Byeolju does not say thank you. It holds its hat on with one flipper the whole way.

choices.text: The snake: "Tell them a rabbit's liver worked last time. Send them to the mountain"

effects.log: Byeolju looks at the snake with deep, tired admiration. "The rabbit said that to me too," it says. "I will try it on the physicians." It does not work. You go down anyway, because now you are curious.

choices.text: The tortoise: draw into the shell, and let Byeolju report that it found only a stone

effects.log: Byeolju sits by the shut shell for a day. Then it says, to the stone, "Good," very quietly, and goes back to the sea alone. You hear later that it reported you dead. It lied to its king for you. You do not forget it.

events.text: The coral hall. The old Dragon King lies on a bed of kelp, grey in the whiskers, his breath coming in slow bubbles. The physicians are a flatfish and an octopus with eight sets of tongs, and they are very interested in your shell. Byeolju stands between you and them in its fraying hat, between its king and its colleague, and trembles.
events.arc: The Dragon King Is Sick Again

choices.text: Offer one shed scute instead of the shell, ground fine, and see what it does

ok.log: The octopus grinds it, grumbling, and the King drinks it in wine, and in the morning sits up and asks for sea grapes. It may have been the scute. It may have been that he wanted to sit up. The physicians write it down as the scute.

fail.log: The scute does nothing. The octopus reaches for the tongs. Byeolju says, very loudly, that the King has asked for sea grapes, which he has not, and in the confusion you are hustled out into the kelp. (-8 health)

choices.text: The snake: read the King's years in the water of his breath, and tell him the truth

effects.log: "You are not sick, Majesty," the snake says. "You are old. A shell will not help that. Nothing will." The hall goes silent. Then the old King laughs, a long rolling laugh of bubbles, and dismisses the physicians, and asks the snake to stay and talk.

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise lies still for the physicians while the snake tells the King what they intend

effects.log: The King hears the whole plan from the snake while the octopus is measuring the tortoise. He sends the physicians to the kitchens. "We do not grind our ministers," he says. "Even the slow ones." Byeolju sits down on the floor of the hall.

events.text: Byeolju finds you that night in the kelp forest at the palace's edge, where you have been told to wait. It has taken off its hat, which you have never seen it do. "I have been at that court all my life," it says. "I have served three kings. I would like to serve this one well. And I would like you to leave, now, through the kelp. I can show you the way."
events.arc: The Dragon King Is Sick Again

choices.text: Go. Byeolju has chosen; let it keep its choice

effects.log: Byeolju takes you through the kelp to the edge of the shelf where the sea goes black and the rivers begin. It does not say goodbye. It puts its hat back on, very straight, and swims back to its king.

choices.text: The snake: "Come with us. You have served enough kings"

effects.log: Byeolju thinks about it for a long time, there in the kelp, hat in its flipper. "No," it says at last. "Somebody has to be there when he ends." The tortoise understands that perfectly, and the snake, to its own surprise, does too.

choices.text: The tortoise: stay, and face the physicians in the morning. Byeolju should not have to lie twice

effects.log: In the morning you are back in the coral hall, and the physicians take a scraping from the edge of one plate, very small, and the King drinks it, and nobody grinds anybody. Byeolju does not speak to you for a week, out of pure relief. (-6 health)

events.text: Years later the old Dragon King dies, in his sleep, in the coral hall, of nothing but a very long life. Byeolju sends word up the river by a carp: the funeral is in the deep, and the King asked for you. You go down. Fish ministers in white, the coral hung with white kelp, the new King young and frightened. Byeolju, at the front, with no hat.
events.arc: The Dragon King Is Sick Again

choices.text: The tortoise: lie at the back of the hall through the whole rite, and watch

effects.log: You watch the old King go down into the trench under the palace, where the old kings go, and the sea above goes quiet for a day. It is an ending. It is Byeolju's, more than yours. You do not write it. You only see it, so that someone did.

choices.text: The snake: speak for the old King, since he asked for you

effects.log: The snake says: he was old, and he knew it, and he was not afraid. That is all it says. The fish ministers do not understand, and the new King does, and Byeolju puts its face down on the coral floor and does not lift it for a long time.

events.text: Byeolju retires. It comes up the river one last time, so slowly that the journey takes a decade, and climbs onto the rock by your ford, and takes off the black gauze hat, and holds it out to you in both flippers. "I am too old for the court," it says. "You are not. Someday the sea will want a minister who has seen how things end. Wear this then."
events.arc: The Dragon King Is Sick Again

choices.text: The tortoise: take the hat, and keep it under your shell for that day

effects.log: The hat lies under your plastron with the other things you keep. Byeolju watches you put it away, nods once, and goes back down the river to wherever old turtles go. You never see it again. You think of it every time you see a carp.

choices.text: The snake: put it on at once, to see how it sits

effects.log: It sits on the snake's head at an angle that makes Byeolju laugh for the first time in two hundred years, a dry little laugh like a hinge. Then the tortoise takes it off the snake and puts it away, for the day it is needed.

events.text: A fever in the valleys downriver, the spotted kind that comes in wet winters and spreads in the thaw. Straw ropes hang across the village gates with red peppers and charcoal twisted in them, to keep the sickness out; they do not. {npc}, the only physician for three valleys, comes down to the frozen river. "Cold kills it," {he} says. "A hard cold, a long one. One more month of winter and it would die in the houses. One more month of winter and the seed rice will rot in the ground before it can be sown. I do not know which to ask for."

choices.text: The tortoise: hold the winter one more month

effects.log: The thaw does not come. The fourth month is a winter month, iron-hard, and the fever dies in the cold houses, family by family. You can feel it dying. You can also feel the seed rice, waiting in the jars, starting to sour.

choices.text: The snake: "Who pays? Ask them that first. Ask the farmers"

effects.log: {npc} goes and asks. It takes a week of meetings in cold rooms. The answer, in the end, is the snake's own question turned round: everyone. They ask for the month anyway. The snake was hoping they would not.

choices.text: Both heads: hold it a fortnight, and break the ice over the seed fields yourself at the end

effects.log: Half the cold and half the cost. The fever is mostly dead; the fields are mostly saved; you spend a week dragging your shell across frozen paddies to break the ground for the sowing, and come back to the river scraped raw. It is not a solution. It is the best compromise two heads could make. (-10 health)

events.text: The fever is gone. In the summer, so is the rice: sown late in cold ground, it comes up thin and yellow and half of it does not come up at all. The valleys that lived through the fever are going to be hungry through the winter. Your winter. You have never been asked for anything by a hungry valley that you could not answer with cold.

choices.text: Drive the fish up into the valley weirs all autumn, every fish in the river

effects.log: The weirs fill so full the nets break. The valleys salt fish all autumn and eat fish all winter and complain about fish all spring, which is the sound of people who did not starve. (-6 health)

choices.text: The snake: "We paid. They paid. That is what we asked them"

effects.log: The snake is right that they were asked. The tortoise lies on the riverbed all winter feeling every empty bowl in the valley, and does not say anything, and the snake feels it not saying anything.

choices.text: Shorten next winter by a month to pay it back

effects.log: The next spring comes a month early and the valleys sow twice. It is not quite repayment. Winters do not balance like ledgers. But it is close.

events.text: A boy of eleven comes down to the river with a pocketful of stones and throws them at the ice, one after another, hard. His family lived through the fever. His grandmother did not live through the hunger after. "You did it," he shouts at the river. "Everyone says the winter went long because of the river. You did it."

choices.text: The tortoise: lie under the ice and let him throw until he is done

effects.log: He throws until dark and then sits on the bank and cries, and then goes home. He comes back every winter for six years to throw stones. In the seventh he comes and only sits.

choices.text: The snake: come up through the ice and tell him the truth: yes. And why

effects.log: The boy does not run. He listens to the whole of it, the fever and the cold and the seed rice and the choice, with a stone still in his fist. At the end he says, "You should have asked my grandmother." The snake has no answer. It keeps that sentence for a thousand years.

events.text: {npc} is old now and has trained nine physicians for the three valleys. {He} comes down to the river one last time, on a stick. "I have been thinking about it for thirty years," {npc} says. "I asked for the cold. You gave it. I still do not know if we were right. Do you?"

choices.text: The snake: "No. That is why we asked who pays"

effects.npcPass: old age, among the nine physicians
effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if that was the answer {he} wanted. Perhaps it was. {He} dies that winter, in a cold that is just the ordinary cold, and the nine physicians carry {him} to the hill.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "We were there. We saw what it cost. That is all I know"

effects.npcPass: old age, among the nine physicians
effects.log: "Then you know more than I do," {npc} says. "I only saw half." {He} sits on the bank until the sun goes, and does not come back. You watch the funeral from the shallows in the spring.

events.text: The snake has asked who pays so many times, about so many winters, that one night under the ice the tortoise finally asks it back: "And us? What do we pay?" The snake does not answer for a long time.

choices.text: The snake: "Everything we hold, we hold for somebody. We pay by remembering them"

effects.log: The tortoise thinks about it until the thaw. It is a better answer than either of you expected. It is also, the tortoise notices, the answer of a creature that has been writing things down.

choices.text: The tortoise answers its own question: "Cold. We pay in cold. It goes into us and does not come out"

effects.log: It is true. Every winter you hold, a little of it stays in you, and your blood moves slower, and your dreams are whiter. Someday you will be more winter than tortoise. The snake shivers, and winds a little tighter. (-6 health)

events.text: The snake, counting years one night, as it does, stops in the middle of a number. "It is time," it says. You both remember: the old woman who talked to the temple pond every evening, when you were small and the pond was your whole world, and the word she gave you for her son, who never came home. She left one thing more, for the family that would come after, as old women do: that a black turtle would come to her line one day, when a woman of it was a grandmother herself, "or she will not understand it." Generations have gone by. There will be such a grandmother now.

choices.text: The tortoise: go and find her, however long the finding takes

effects.log: You set off for the old temple pond, three rivers and centuries away. The snake says she is probably dead. The tortoise says then you will find that out properly.

choices.text: The snake: "She is probably dead. People are"

effects.log: The snake says it, and the tortoise turns toward the temple anyway, and the snake goes along because it goes where the tortoise goes, and because it would very much like to be wrong.

events.text: The temple pond has silted into a lotus marsh and the village beside it has moved twice. The temple is still there, smaller, with one old monk and a register of offerings going back three hundred years, names and villages and gifts of rice, in a chest by the altar. The monk does not mind a tortoise reading over his shoulder. He is very short-sighted.

choices.text: The snake: read the register, every name, until you find the family

ok.log: Centuries of rice offerings, and there she is: a woman of the line, married into a village four valleys east, who still sends a sack of rice to the temple every autumn in her grandmother's name. The snake was wrong. It is delighted.

fail.log: The handwriting defeats even the snake. The monk, who it turns out is not so short-sighted, says: "The rice from the east? Four valleys over. Every autumn. Her grandmother's name." He does not ask why a turtle wants to know.

choices.text: The tortoise: wait by the temple until someone brings an offering in the old woman's name

effects.log: It takes two autumns. Then a grandson comes up the path with a sack of rice and says the old woman's name to the monk, and you follow him home, four valleys east, at the speed of a tortoise, which is how you arrive a year after him.

events.text: {npc} is washing clothes at the stream with a laundry bat, white-haired, with three grandchildren splashing on the bank. {He} looks down into the water and sees a black shell as wide as a threshing floor, and two heads, and does not scream. "Grandmother said," {npc} says slowly. "Grandmother always said the pond would come."

choices.text: The tortoise: let the snake say it exactly as the old woman gave it, every word

effects.log: The snake speaks the old woman's word exactly, in the old woman's own odd turn of phrase, even the hard part, I was not angry, which the old woman did not quite mean. {npc} sits down on the stones and laughs and cries at once. "Yes," {npc} says. "Yes, now I understand it." A word kept, centuries late and exactly on time. It goes on your back.

choices.text: The snake: say it, but kinder. Leave out the hard part

effects.log: The snake leaves out the hard part, I was not angry, and puts in a blessing the old woman never said. {npc} weeps with gratitude. The tortoise says nothing, and the plate on its back cracks in the first frost, and it goes on saying nothing all winter.

choices.text: Both heads: say it exactly, and then stay and listen to {his} whole life, as the pond once did

effects.log: The word, exactly. Then a whole autumn at the stream while {npc} tells you everything, from the beginning, the way {his} grandmother once told the pond. A word kept, and a word received. It goes on your back.

choices.text: Say it, exactly, and let it be only spoken; your back has no room for it

effects.log: {npc} hears it, and understands it, and that is enough. Not every kept word needs a plate. Some only need a stream and an old woman and the right year.

events.text: {npc} brings the grandchildren down to the stream on a summer evening, all of them, nine, and sits them in a row on the bank. "This is the pond," {npc} tells them. "It knew the first of our grandmothers. It came four valleys to bring me a word. If you ever have a word that has to wait a long time, this is who you give it to."

choices.text: The snake: let each child give you a word, a small one, for practice

effects.log: Nine small words: a hidden marble, a dead puppy's name, a promise to a best friend. You keep every one. Forty years later you deliver four of them, which astonishes four grown people very much.

choices.text: The tortoise: just let them look at you a long time

effects.log: Nine children look at a tortoise as big as a threshing floor for as long as children can look at anything, which is not long. Then they go back to splashing. One of them, the smallest, keeps looking.

events.text: {npc} dies in the winter, very old, and asks to be buried on the hill above the stream, facing the water. The funeral comes down the path in white hemp with the bier and the bell. The grandchildren, grown now, stop at the stream and pour a cup of wine into it, for the pond.

choices.text: Watch the whole rite from the shallows, and remember it

effects.log: You watch until the last mourner goes back down the hill. The old woman and a descendant of the same house, centuries apart, both talked to you. Both of them are on your back now, in the same plate, side by side.

choices.text: The snake: say the grandmother's word once more, quietly, over the grave

effects.log: Nobody hears it but the hill. That is all right. It was never really for anyone else.

events.text: A pool upstream, at the head of a gorge, under a fall. Something lives in it: a serpent thick as a pillar, hornless, old, with a pearl-grey eye. An Imugi, waiting to become a dragon. It looks at your snake for a long time and says, in a voice like water in a cave: "I was a black snake once. Smaller than you. I went up a river to a pool and waited. Come. Be a dragon." The tortoise hears every word.
events.arc: The Imugi in the Next Pool

choices.text: The snake: go closer, and listen

effects.log: The snake stretches out over the water as far as it can go without leaving the shell, and listens to the Imugi all night. The tortoise, who cannot stretch anywhere, waits on the rock and listens to the snake listening.

choices.text: The tortoise: turn and go back down the gorge, now

effects.log: You turn round on the rock and go, and the snake comes, because it has to. It does not forgive the tortoise for a year. It does not forget the pool for a great deal longer.

choices.text: Both heads: stay, both of you, and hear the whole offer together

effects.log: You hear it together: the pool, the pearl, the thousand years, the one witness who must see it rise and call it a dragon. The Imugi seems surprised that the tortoise is listening too. "Turtles are for carrying," it says.

events.text: The snake goes back to the pool. Not leaving: it cannot leave, it is wound round you. But every night it stretches toward the gorge, and the tortoise goes there, because there is nowhere else for the tortoise to go when the snake pulls. "And the tortoise?" the snake asks the Imugi one night. "What happens to the tortoise?"
events.arc: The Imugi in the Next Pool

choices.text: Let the Imugi answer

effects.log: "It lives a long time," says the Imugi, "as a turtle. In a mill pond, probably. They always end up in mill ponds." It does not say it unkindly. That is the worst part. The snake does not ask anything else that night.

choices.text: The tortoise speaks to the Imugi itself, for once: "I would wait for it. In the mill pond"

effects.log: The Imugi blinks its pearl-grey eye, slowly. Nobody, it says, has ever said that about it. The snake hears it too. It winds one coil tighter, without meaning to, and the tortoise feels it.

events.text: The night of the Imugi's rising: a storm over the gorge, lightning walking down the cliffs, and the great serpent climbing the waterfall into the cloud. Halfway up, a charcoal-burner on the ridge sees it in a flash of lightning and shouts, as people do: "Look, a big worm!" The serpent stops. It hangs on the fall. Then it falls, the whole length of it, back into the pool.
events.arc: The Imugi in the Next Pool

choices.text: The snake: go to it, in the pool, and stay with it till morning

effects.log: The snake lies along the Imugi's great grey length in the black water all night and says nothing, which the snake has never done for anybody. In the morning the Imugi says: "Another thousand years." The snake says: "Yes." Then you go home.

choices.text: The tortoise: look at the charcoal-burner, and understand what a witness is for

effects.log: One word. One man on a ridge, who saw it and called it a worm, and a thousand years fell back into a pool. The tortoise understands, that night, exactly how much a witness weighs. It is the most frightening thing it has ever understood.

events.text: The snake has gone very quiet since the night of the storm. It lies loose on the shell, two coils where there were three, and looks up the gorge at dusk. One night it says, not to the tortoise, to the dark: "It would have been a dragon if the man had said dragon. One word." Then: "Would you say it? If it were me?"
events.arc: The Imugi in the Next Pool

choices.text: The tortoise: "Yes. Dragon. And then I would go to the mill pond"

effects.log: The snake is silent a long time. Then it winds the third coil back round the shell, slowly, and says that a mill pond sounds very dull, and that it would not want to leave the tortoise there with nobody to cheat at stones. It does not go up the gorge again.

choices.text: The tortoise: "I do not know." It is the truth

effects.log: The snake nods, as much as a snake can. It respects the truth; it has had to live wound round it for centuries. But it goes on looking up the gorge at dusk. The pool is still there. It will always be there.

choices.text: Both heads: "We would be a strange dragon. We should try being a strange tortoise first"

effects.log: The snake laughs, and that is the end of it, mostly. There will be nights when it looks up the gorge. There will not be nights when it goes.

events.text: Long years on, the pool at the head of the gorge is empty. A herd boy says a great serpent went up in a storm last summer, and the old men on the ridge called it a dragon, all of them, at the tops of their voices, because their grandfathers had told them about the time a charcoal-burner called it a worm.
events.arc: The Imugi in the Next Pool

choices.text: The snake: go up the gorge and look at the empty pool, once

effects.log: The water is very still. A scale the size of a gong lies on the bottom, grey, with a little pearl-light still in it. The snake looks at it for an hour and comes back to the shell without a word, and winds tight.

choices.text: The tortoise: go up the ridge instead, and thank the old men

effects.log: Three old men on a ridge, very surprised to be thanked by a tortoise as big as a threshing floor. They will tell it to their grandchildren, who will not believe it, which is how things are kept.

events.text: Alchemists of a sect, in grey robes, with copper tongs, a bronze mirror on a pole and a brazier on a sledge. Their founder's book says the Black Tortoise Iron Canon, the northern method that hardens the body like a shell, was first read in the grain of a living thousand-year tortoise. The best way to read grain, the book says, is on a plate that has been taken off.

choices.text: The tortoise: draw in, all the way, and be a stone they cannot open

effects.log: They try the tongs. They try the brazier under you, until the river puts it out. They try prayers. By spring they decide you are a rock that looks like a tortoise, which, from the inside, you nearly are.

choices.text: The snake: come out of the water at the one holding the mirror

effects.log: The mirror goes into the river and its holder goes into the snow. The rest of them decide the canon can be studied from the old book after all. The snake keeps the mirror. It likes looking at itself.

choices.text: Let them read one plate through the mirror, without touching, and send them away

ok.log: You turn one plate to the mirror and they copy the grain onto paper all night by torchlight, astonished. They go home with the most accurate Iron Canon in the murim, and without your shell. The snake calls it a fair trade. The tortoise calls it a narrow one.

fail.log: Reading is not enough for them; they want the plate. The tongs get a grip on the edge of one scute before the snake bites the hand. You go down into the deep bleeding, and the sect knows exactly where you live now. (-12 health)

events.text: The sect sends one apprentice this time, alone, with a brush and paper and no tongs: {npc}, sixteen, terrified, who has been told to read the canon in the living shell and come back with it, or not come back. {He} kneels on the frozen bank with the paper shaking and says to the ice, very politely: "Please. I only need to look."

choices.text: The tortoise: come up and turn every plate to {him}, slowly, for as long as {he} needs

effects.log: It takes the whole winter. {npc} copies the grain of thirteen plates onto paper, frost on {his} eyebrows, and at the end understands something about the canon that nobody in the sect has understood: it is not a method for hardening. It is a method for waiting.

choices.text: The snake: ask {him} what the sect will do to {him} if {he} goes back without it

effects.log: {npc} tells you. The snake listens, then turns one plate to the paper itself and says: "That one. It is enough to save your life and not enough to take mine. Copy it well." {npc} does.

events.text: {npc} comes back twenty years later, an elder of the sect now, in grey robes with a gold border, alone again. "They want me to lead the next hunt," {he} says. "Tongs and braziers. The whole shell this time. I told them the canon on your back is already in our library, in my hand. They said the hand of an apprentice is not the grain of a shell. I have come to tell you I will not lead it. And that someone else will."

choices.text: The tortoise: thank {him}, and go down into the deep for a decade

effects.log: You go down so deep the hunt finds nothing but cold water. {npc} is stripped of the gold border for refusing, and takes the grey robe back without complaint, and teaches the canon {his} own way for the rest of {his} life: as a method for waiting.

choices.text: The snake: tell {him} the hunt's route through the gorge, and where the ice will be thin

effects.log: The hunt goes through the gorge on the ice where the snake said, and the ice is thin where the snake said, and nobody drowns, quite. They do not come back. The tortoise thinks the snake enjoyed that more than it should have.

events.text: They come at night with the brazier already lit, a dozen of them on the ice with tongs and hooks and a net of iron chain, and a talisman on every link: they mean to haul you out whole and take the shell at their leisure. The ice under them is yours. So is the cold.

choices.text: Fight them on the ice, both heads

ok.log: The shell takes the hooks and the snake takes the hands, and the net goes into the river with three alchemists still holding it, and is let go of just in time. The rest run. The brazier rolls hissing into a hole in the ice.

fail.deathCause: the iron net and the brazier of a sect that wanted the Black Tortoise Iron Canon in its own hands

choices.text: Freeze the river so hard the ice splits under the brazier

effects.log: The cold goes up through the ice like a shout and the ice cracks in a star under the brazier. Fire and chains and alchemists go into the black water, and you let every one of them climb out again, slowly, half frozen. (-6 health)

choices.text: The tortoise: go down under the deep ice and wait

effects.log: They fish for you all night and catch an old millstone. You hear them arguing on the ice above about whose map it was. In the morning they go.

events.text: The year the snake read. In the house above the ford an old salt-carrier is dying, ninety-one, the oldest man in the county, with his sons around the mat. The Dipper, the mansion of lifespans. You lie under the window in the dark and hear the breath go slow. The snake, beside you, says very quietly that it could ask the two old men on the mountain for one more year. It has done stranger things.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie still and hear the last breath. It is his

effects.log: He goes a little before dawn, easily, in the middle of a sentence about salt. You hear it end. It is the plainest ending you have ever witnessed, and the truest. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: go up the mountain tonight and ask for one more year

effects.log: The snake goes, and comes back at dawn with a look you have never seen on it. The old man lives one more year, and spends it teaching his grandson the salt roads, and dies in the spring. There is no ending here for a plate now. There is a grandson who knows the roads.

choices.text: Both heads: hear it to the end, and then go and tell the sons he was not afraid

effects.log: He was not. You tell them through the snake, from the dark under the window, and the eldest son weeps with relief. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A girl of nineteen, a ferryman's daughter, is going to drown at the ford this spring; the snake read it in the ice twenty years ago, before she was born, and here it is, the flood and the overturned boat and her hand in the brown water. The Dipper: a lifespan ending, or rewritten. You are three strokes away.

choices.text: The tortoise: you came to witness. Witness

effects.log: You do not move. It is the hardest stillness of your life, and when it is over the river is only a river again. The snake does not speak to you for a year. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: Rewrite it: come up under her and carry her to the bank

effects.log: She comes up on a black shell, coughing, and is hauled out by her father. She lives to ninety-nine, which the snake insists on calling a coincidence. Nineteen to ninety-nine. There is nothing here for a plate. The tortoise came to write, and does not mind at all.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake takes her to the bank while the tortoise watches the flood take the boat

effects.log: The boat goes under, and the girl does not. The ending you witness is a smaller one than the snake read: a boat. Still an ending. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: The old rope bridge over the gorge, the one the snake read would go: the first spring flood, and a salt merchant's mule train halfway across when the downstream rope begins to fray. The Ox, mansion of passes and bridges. A crossing is ending. Whether anyone is on it when it does is not yet written.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch the bridge go, and the crossing with it

effects.log: The last mule reaches the far side. Then the rope parts and the bridge folds into the gorge like a dropped sash, plank by plank. You watch every plank. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: Lie down in the gorge as a ford, so there is still a crossing when the bridge is gone

effects.log: The bridge goes, and the next morning there is a black shell in the shallows that the mules can walk over, and do, for a whole season, until the new bridge is built. The crossing did not end. There is no plate.

choices.text: Both heads: hold the frayed rope with the snake until the mules are over, then let it go and watch

effects.log: The snake holds the rope round a rock for as long as a snake can, which is long enough. Then it lets go, and you both watch the bridge fall, empty. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: The ferry at the next ford is closing. The ferryman is old and his sons have gone to the city, and the county is building a stone bridge upstream. Tonight is the last crossing: the ferryman takes his own family over, and then rows back alone, and ties up the boat for the last time. The Ox: a crossing, ending.

choices.text: The tortoise: lie under the ferry for its last crossing, and feel it go

effects.log: The boat goes over and back above you, slow and heavy, and then the rope goes slack. Nobody will cross here again. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: speak to the ferryman, and ask him to keep the boat for floods

effects.log: He keeps it, under a straw roof on the bank, and in the great flood of the next decade, when the stone bridge goes under, the old ferry crosses again. The crossing did not end. No plate, and a village that got across.

choices.text: Both heads: steady the boat on its last crossing, so the old man's hands do not have to

effects.log: The ferryman notices. He looks down into the water for a long time, and then says: "Thank you, then," to the river, for every year. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A wedding on the far bank, and the snake read it would be broken: the groom's family has found a richer match, and tonight, the night before the rites, the go-between will come to the bride's gate with the betrothal letter to return it. The Girl, mansion of marriages made and broken. The bride is sitting on the riverbank in the dark.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch the letter come back, and the bride's face

effects.log: The go-between comes, and goes. The bride does not weep; she folds the returned letter very small and drops it in the river, and it comes down to you. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: go to the groom's house in the night and tell him what his family is doing

effects.log: The groom did not know. There is a great deal of shouting in a rich house before dawn, and the wedding goes ahead the next day, a little late. A marriage made, not broken. There is nothing here for your plate now; there is a bride who will never know why.

choices.text: Both heads: let it break, and then send the bride a carp in the morning, the old sign of a good match to come

effects.log: The letter comes back. In the morning the bride finds a great golden carp on her doorstep, which in that village means a better marriage is coming. It does, four years later. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: An old couple, married sixty years, who met on this riverbank as children. The wife died in the spring. Tonight, the husband walks down to the water with her silver hairpin and a bowl of rice wine, and the snake read long ago that this is the night the marriage ends, really ends, when the last one who remembers the wedding lets go of it.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch him pour the wine and drop the pin into the water

effects.log: He pours the wine slowly, and says her name, and drops the hairpin into the dark. It comes down onto your shell and stays there. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: bring the hairpin back up to him on the bank

effects.log: He finds the pin on the stones at his feet in the morning, dry. He takes it home, and keeps it, and talks to it every evening for the six years he has left. The marriage did not end that night. No plate.

choices.text: Both heads: catch the pin, and tell him you will keep it

effects.log: "Good," he says, when the snake tells him. "She liked the river." He goes home lighter. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A funeral procession comes down to the river at dawn, as the snake read: bier and white hemp and paper banners and the bell, and the mourners keening on the path. A magistrate the whole county loved, who died owing nobody anything. The Emptiness, mansion of mourning. You lie in the shallows where the procession must cross.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch the whole procession cross, every mourner, to the grave

effects.log: It takes all morning. You count nobody and see everybody. When the last mourner is over the ford you lie a while longer, for the magistrate. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: stop the bier at the ford; the snake has seen the magistrate breathe

effects.log: It was not death. It was a sleeping sickness, and the snake had seen it in the ice and not believed it. The magistrate sits up on the bier in the middle of the river, and the mourners scatter screaming. He lives eleven more years. There is no ending to write, and a county that is still talking about it.

choices.text: Both heads: hold the ford calm under the bearers, so nobody stumbles with the bier

effects.log: The bearers cross dry-footed in water that should be waist-deep. Afterwards they swear the magistrate himself held the river still. You let them. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A tomb is being closed: a mound on the hill above the river, the stone door being rolled across, the last lamp inside left burning for the dead. The snake read it decades ago in a crack in the ice shaped like a door. The Emptiness: tombs and mourning. The mourners are gone. Only the tomb-builders are left, and you.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch the door close, and the last light go out under it

effects.log: The stone grinds home. A thin line of lamplight under it for an hour, then nothing. You lie on the bank until morning. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: slip in under the door before it closes, and look at the painted walls

effects.log: The snake goes in and is nearly shut in, and comes out with the last of the light, full of what it saw: a dragon, a tiger, a bird, and on the north wall, two heads. The builders, startled, leave the door a hand's width open for a week. The ending is put off. No plate.

choices.text: Both heads: lay a river stone at the door, for whoever is inside

effects.log: A black stone, smooth, from the bottom of your river, at the foot of the door. The builders leave it there. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A great house in the county town falls, as the snake read: the merchant's family that built it is ruined by a debt and a seal, and tonight the bailiffs come, and the roof ridge that took three generations to raise is pulled down for the beams. The Rooftop, mansion of roofs and treasuries. You are in the garden pond.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch it come down, beam by beam, until morning

effects.log: The ridge-beam comes down at dawn. The family stands in the courtyard in their good clothes with nothing in their hands. You see all of it. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: show the youngest son where his grandfather buried the family silver, under this very pond

effects.log: The son digs, at midnight, with his hands, and pays the debt before the bailiffs reach the roof. The house stands. No plate, and a family that never knows who told the boy.

choices.text: Both heads: watch it fall, and then lead the family out through the garden gate before the bailiffs see them

effects.log: The roof comes down. The family goes out by the back, with the grandmother on the eldest son's back, and is gone by daylight. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: The village's great rice store, the one the whole valley paid into for forty years against famine, burns tonight, as the snake read in a crack in the ice twelve years ago. A lamp kicked over by a drunk watchman. The Rooftop: a treasury falling. You are in the millstream beside it.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch it burn, every sack

effects.log: You watch until the last of the roof falls in. The valley stands round it in silence. The snake says that is the worst sound it has ever heard. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: Freeze the millstream and flood the store with ice before the fire reaches the grain

effects.log: The water comes up out of the millstream in a white wave and the fire hisses out in an hour. Half the roof is gone. None of the rice. No plate. The watchman swears off drink for the rest of his life.

choices.text: Both heads: wake the watchman before the lamp goes over

effects.log: The snake hisses at his ear and he sits up and knocks the lamp over anyway, of course, and the store burns. But the watchman got out. You saw all of it. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: The army's works on the river plain, the great earthen fort a governor built with ten thousand labourers to hold the northern road: abandoned tonight, as the snake read, by order of a new king who does not want it. The Encampment, mansion of an army's works ending. The garrison marches out at dusk and leaves the gate open.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch the last soldier go, and the gate stand open in the snow

effects.log: The gate stands open all night. By morning snow has drifted into the yard and a fox has gone in to look. The fort is ended. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: speak to the garrison commander: the northern road is not safe yet

effects.log: The commander listens to a voice from the river, which commanders usually do not, and sends a message to the capital, and stays. Three years later the northern road is attacked and the fort holds it. No ending, and a road that stayed open.

choices.text: Both heads: watch them go, and then close the gate behind them with your shell, for the fox's sake

effects.log: The gate swings shut on its own, the soldiers think, looking back from the road. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: The great dyke on the lower river, built by corvée in the time of someone's grandfather: tonight, as the snake read, it will go in the spring flood. The labourers' camp is long gone; the villages behind it are not. The Encampment: great earthworks ending. The water is already over the top in two places.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch it go, as you came to

effects.log: It goes at midnight, in one long roar. The villages behind it had been warned by the headman, who had been warned by nobody he can name. You see it all. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: Lie down in the breach as it opens, and hold it till the villages are out

effects.log: You hold a river with your shell until dawn, and the villages walk out onto the hills with their oxen and their ancestors' tablets. Then you let go. The dyke stands, broken but standing, and is mended in the summer. No plate. The shell aches for a year.

choices.text: Both heads: wake the villages first, the snake at every door, then come back and watch

effects.log: Every door, a hiss and a voice. By the time the dyke goes, the houses are empty. You come back to the bank in time to see it break. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A library burns, as the snake read: the private library of a scholar's family in the hills, four generations of books in a tiled pavilion, and tonight a spark from the kitchen. The Wall, mansion of writing and heaven's archive of books. You are in the lotus pond in front of it.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch every book burn, and remember every title you can read

effects.log: You watch it all, and the snake reads the spines through the flames until they are gone. You know forty-one titles you did not know yesterday. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: wake the scholar's grandson in time to carry out the oldest chest

effects.log: The grandson carries out one chest, the oldest, with the family genealogy in it and three books nobody else in the kingdom owns. The pavilion burns, but the library did not end. No plate.

choices.text: Both heads: wake the grandson, and then watch the rest go

effects.log: One chest out, and the rest burns, and you see it all. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: A monk is burning a book, as the snake read: an old sutra commentary in the temple by the river, the last copy, which the abbot has declared heretical. A small fire in a stone basin in the courtyard, at night, one page at a time. The Wall: a book lost. You are in the temple's cistern.

choices.text: The tortoise: watch every page go, and read each one as it burns

effects.log: You read it, page by page, as the monk feeds it to the fire. It is not heretical. It is only difficult. You have it now, all of it, somewhere under the plates. (Write it on the shell.)

choices.text: The snake: hiss from the cistern, so the monk runs, and the last third of the book survives

effects.log: The monk runs. The last third of the commentary lies by the basin, scorched, until a novice hides it in the rafters. It is copied long afterwards. No ending to write.

choices.text: Both heads: let it burn, and ask the monk afterwards, through the snake, what it said

effects.log: The monk tells you, weeping. He had read it. He agreed with it. The abbot did not. (Write it on the shell.)

events.text: They come down to the water at dusk, as the word said they would: a soldier, very old, in a patched army coat forty years out of date, who has walked from the far end of the kingdom because something told him to come to this river. He looks at the water as if he knows exactly what is in it.
events.arc: The One the Word Was For

choices.text: The tortoise: let him look a while before the snake speaks

effects.log: He looks for a long time. Then he sits down on a stone, as if he had all the years in the world, which he does not. When you are ready, Carry the Word.

choices.text: The snake: rehearse the word once more under the water, exactly

effects.log: Every word, every pause, as it was given, forty years ago, by someone who is dead. The snake gets it perfect. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: A woman of seventy comes down the bank on a grandson's arm and stops at the very edge of the water. "I dreamed of a black tortoise for nine nights," she says. "My mother always said a black tortoise would bring me something one day. I thought it was a story. I am too old for stories now, so I came."
events.arc: The One the Word Was For

choices.text: The tortoise: rise slowly, so she can see you are real

effects.log: She sees the shell come up out of the water like an island, and puts out one hand, and touches it, and laughs. "Well," she says. "Go on, then." (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

choices.text: The snake: ask her to sit down first. The word is not a small one

effects.log: She sits. The grandson holds her hand. It is a good thing she sat. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: The word you are carrying falls due, and the one it is for is here: a magistrate, middle-aged and tired, on a tour of the river villages, who has stopped his sedan chair at the ford for no reason he can name. The word is from someone he wronged, long ago. It is not a comfortable word.
events.arc: The One the Word Was For

choices.text: The tortoise: it must be said as it was given. Prepare to say it all

effects.log: The tortoise holds the hard part ready, the way you hold a cold stone in your mouth. (Carry the Word: deliver it, exactly.)

choices.text: The snake: it could be said more gently. Think about how

effects.log: The snake turns the word over all night, looking for a softer edge. There is always a softer edge. That is the danger. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: A child comes down to the water: eight years old, alone, very serious. The word you carry was given to you for a grandmother, by her own grandmother, but the grandmother died last winter, and this is her granddaughter's daughter, who says: "Grandma said if the turtle ever came, I should listen for her."
events.arc: The One the Word Was For

choices.text: The tortoise: then the word is for the child now. Words go down like rivers

effects.log: You give it to the child instead. She will carry it longer than you did. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

choices.text: The snake: ask the child what her grandmother was like, first

effects.log: The child tells you for an hour: the cooking, the scolding, the songs. By the end the word fits her like it was always meant to. (Carry the Word: deliver it.)

events.text: {npc}, a general of the north in a plain coat, kneels on the bank in the dark. "Tomorrow I lead an army across the frontier," {he} says, "and I will not come back. Everyone says so; I say so. My daughter is three. When the child is grown, say I did not want to go. Say I went anyway. Both. The child should have both."

choices.text: The snake: promise both halves, exactly

effects.log: The snake repeats it back: did not want to, went anyway. {npc} nods, satisfied, and goes up the bank to {his} army. You will carry it for years. You will not change it.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "Say it yourself. Come back"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, short. "If I come back, you can give it back to me," {he} says. You take it anyway. The tortoise hopes, very hard, to have to give it back.

choices.text: Both heads: take it, and ask for one more thing: something the child can recognise you by

effects.log: {npc} thinks, and gives you a song: the one {he} sings at night to the child, about a fox and a well. So when the time comes, the snake will sing it first. The tortoise thinks that is the best part of the word.

events.text: {npc}, a master of the high realms, white-haired and very straight, sits on the bank with {his} sword across {his} knees. "They say the snake reads where things end," {he} says. "Read mine. I would like to know where. And I would like the tortoise to be there."

choices.text: The snake: read it in the water, and tell {him} truly

ok.log: A pass in the western hills, in snow, in twenty-two years, at the end of a duel {he} will win. {npc} listens without moving. "Good," {he} says. "Winning is good." Then: "And the tortoise?" The tortoise says, through the snake, that it will be there.

fail.log: The water shows nothing, or too much: a pass, a bed, a boat. The snake says so honestly. {npc} laughs. "So it is not written yet," {he} says. "Better." {He} asks the tortoise to come anyway, when it hears.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "I will be there. Do not ask where"

effects.log: {npc} looks at the water a long time, then bows to it, very low, the bow of one master to another. "Then I will not," {he} says. You will have to find out on your own. The tortoise is good at that.

events.text: {npc}, a merchant's widow who runs the family's river trade now, comes down to the ford with a ledger. "My husband's partner cheated us thirty years ago," {he} says, "and died rich. That partner's son is a boy now. When the son is forty, and has a family, and has been cheated in turn, tell the son what the father did. Not before. The son would not understand before."

choices.text: The tortoise: take it, exactly as given, and keep it the full forty years

effects.log: It is a cold word, carefully made. You take it the way you would take a sealed jar of something that keeps. The snake asks whether it is a gift or a curse. "Both," says {npc}. "Like most true things."

choices.text: The snake: ask whether {he} would like it to be a kinder word, by then

effects.log: {npc} looks at the snake with real respect. "No," {he} says. "But thank you for asking. You will be tempted. Do not." The snake promises. The tortoise is not sure the snake knows yet how hard that promise is.

events.text: {npc}, a weaver from a village with a war between it and the next, comes to the river at night and kneels where the ferry used to land. "There is someone on the far bank," {he} says. "We were to be married. The war closed the river. If it ever opens, tell them I waited. Not that I waited for ever. That I waited as long as I could. That is the true one."

choices.text: The snake: carry it, and carry it exactly: as long as I could

effects.log: The snake says it back three times to get the weight right. "As long as I could." {npc} nods at the third. It is the hardest small word you have ever been given. It is also the kindest.

choices.text: The tortoise: swim it across tonight. Rivers are not closed to you

effects.log: You go across under the sentries' boats and up to the far bank, and the snake finds the right door by dawn. The answer comes back the next night: wait a little longer, then. You carry that too. (-6 health)

events.text: {npc}, an old king of a small kingdom, has come to the riverbank in disguise, with one guard, at night. "I have a word for the Dragon King of the sea," {he} says. "My great-grandfather made a promise to the deep: no fishing in the spawning month. My son will break it; I can see it already. Tell the deep that I am sorry, now, before it happens. And that it was not the whole family."

choices.text: The snake: carry it down to the coral hall, with the apology first

effects.log: The Dragon King hears it in the coral hall with that great head on one side. "Apologising for a sin the prince has not committed yet," says the Dragon King. "That is new." The memory stays, thirty years later, when the son breaks the promise, and the deep is gentler than it would have been.

choices.text: The tortoise: carry it, and then go and watch the son, so you can tell the deep the whole truth

effects.log: You watch the son for years. The son breaks the promise in the spawning month, exactly as the old king saw. You carry both down to the deep: the apology, and the breaking. The Dragon King says that is the most complete report the deep has ever had.

events.text: {npc}, a woman of the ice-cutting crews, red-handed from the cold, has a word for nobody yet born. "My family has cut the river ice for six generations," {he} says. "Someday there will be no more cutting; I can feel it coming. When it stops, tell the last of us that the first of us were proud of it."

choices.text: The tortoise: take it, for as long as it takes

effects.log: It may take centuries. The tortoise does not mind that at all. The snake asks how you will know which one is the last. "We will know," the tortoise says. It is usually right about that sort of thing.

choices.text: The snake: ask what the first of them were like

effects.log: {npc} tells you about a great-great-grandmother with a saw taller than a door, who sang while cutting. The snake memorises the song. When the time comes, it will deliver that too.

events.text: {npc} is the daughter of the general who knelt on this bank years ago: grown, sharp-faced, in a soldier's coat of {his} own. {He} has come because {his} mother told {him} a story about a river. The snake sings the song about the fox and the well first, the way the general asked, and {npc} goes white.

choices.text: The snake: give {him} both halves, exactly: did not want to go; went anyway

effects.npcPass: a long life after, a soldier like the general
effects.log: {npc} hears both, and stands very still for a long time, and then says, "Yes. That was my father," and goes back up the bank with a set face. A word kept, both halves. It goes on your back.

choices.text: The snake: give {him} only the first half. {He} is a soldier; the second would hurt

effects.npcPass: a long life after, a soldier like the general
effects.log: Did not want to go. {npc} weeps, grateful, and leaves gentler than {he} came. The tortoise was given two halves and watched one delivered. The plate cracks in the first frost.

choices.text: Give {him} both halves, and let it be only spoken; your back is full of words

effects.npcPass: a long life after, a soldier like the general
effects.log: {npc} hears it. That is what it was for. Not every word needs a plate.

events.text: {npc}, a grandmaster who stands at the very top of the murim, walks out onto the river ice in a black coat with a sword at the hip and stops above you. "I have come to duel the Black Warrior," {he} says. "The north's tortoise. They say you will be." The snake looks at the tortoise. The tortoise looks at the snake. "Which of us?" the snake asks.

choices.text: The tortoise, through the snake: "Neither. We do not duel. We outlast"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, and sits down on the ice to think about that, and is still sitting there at dusk. "I have never been refused like that," {he} says. "I will come back when you are the Black Warrior." {He} means it.

choices.text: The snake: "Me. The tortoise is busy"

ok.log: Three exchanges, the sword against the snake, faster than anyone on the bank can see. On the third the snake has the sword-hand in its mouth, very gently. {npc} bows over it. "Next time," {he} says, "both of you."

fail.log: The sword finds the snake's neck on the second exchange, flat, not edge. {npc} lowers it. "Not yet," {he} says, not unkindly. "One head is not enough. Come back with two." The snake does not speak for a month. (-15 health)

choices.text: Both heads: "Both of us, or neither. Choose"

effects.log: {npc} looks from one head to the other for a long time. "Neither, then," {he} says. "Two I cannot read. I will come back when I can." {He} has not come back yet. The snake considers this a win.

events.text: The first hard frost, and the cracked plate on your back aches. Not a pain exactly: a wrongness, like a word said slightly off in a song everyone knows. The tortoise feels it all winter. The snake feels the tortoise feeling it, which is worse.

choices.text: The tortoise: resolve to go back to that place and find the truth, someday soon

effects.log: Someday soon, the tortoise says, the way tortoises do. But it means it. (Write on the Shell: go back and mend it.)

choices.text: The snake: say it is only a little crack, and nobody will ever read it

effects.log: Somebody will read it. The snake knows that. Everything on your back is going to be read, one day, aloud, by someone who is not on your side. It says the other thing anyway, because the frost hurts.

events.text: In a long dream under the ice, you see the northern sky, and the seven dark stars over the pole, and the empty seat. And on your own back, one plate that glows wrong: a little too bright, like a lamp with the wick turned up to hide a smudge on the glass. You wake with the crack aching.

choices.text: The tortoise: count the years until you can go back and mend it

effects.log: The snake counts them for you, because it is better at counting, and does not round down. It is the closest thing to an apology it has.

choices.text: The snake: admit, aloud, that it should not have written it

effects.log: It takes the snake most of a winter to say it. When it does, the ache does not go, but it changes: it is now an ache you both have, instead of one you have and one you cause.

events.text: The snake is restless. It wakes before you, goes out on its own at night as far as a snake wound round a shell can go, comes back late. It has started telling stories again, but they are all about places it has never been, and it tells them to the river, not to you.

choices.text: Let the Heads Talk: set out the stones on the riverbed tonight

effects.log: The snake comes to the board late, and plays badly, and cheats worse. But it plays. By the end of the game it has told you one of the stories, and that one is about you.

choices.text: The tortoise: go where it wants to go, for once, without asking why

effects.log: Three days upriver to a pool the snake has heard of. It is only a pool. The snake is so surprised you came that it forgets why it wanted to. (-4 health)

events.text: The tortoise, this time, is the one who will not talk. It has drawn in for a whole season, deep inside the shell, where the snake cannot follow, and lies there like a stone while the snake lies outside on the riverbed and talks to nobody. You have been one body for centuries. It has never felt so much like two.

choices.text: The snake: tap on the shell, once a day, until the tortoise comes out

effects.log: Ninety-one days. On the ninety-second the head comes out, and looks at the snake, and goes back in. On the ninety-third it stays out. Neither of you mentions the ninety-one days. You will both remember them.

choices.text: Let it be. A tortoise has the right to its shell

effects.log: The season passes. The tortoise comes out in its own time, and the snake has learned to be alone, a little. Neither of you is sure that is a good thing to have learned.
